differentiation.title: My reading and writing map
differentiation.activity: Students complete a brief inventory of reading and writing experiences, interests, strengths, and challenges. They examine examples of specific goals, develop one reading goal and one writing goal, and identify a practical action for each. Students select a short text that connects with an identified interest.
differentiation.scaffolds: Visual interest inventory, genre examples, teacher-modeled goals, sentence frames, individual conference.
differentiation.success: Identify at least two personal preferences, create two actionable goals, and explain one purposeful text choice.
differentiation.materials: Reading and writing inventory; goal-setting template; curated text choices.

differentiation.title: Literary community workshop
differentiation.activity: Students read a common short story or a choice of related short texts. Small groups establish discussion norms, share interpretations supported by evidence, and practice active listening. Students then exchange brief written responses, offer specific feedback, and complete a reflection on how discussion or feedback changed their thinking.
differentiation.scaffolds: Discussion norms, conversation stems, feedback protocol, reflection prompts.
differentiation.success: Contribute an evidence-based interpretation, respond respectfully to another perspective, offer actionable feedback, and explain one insight gained through participation.
differentiation.materials: Short literary texts; discussion guide; peer feedback form; reflection journal.

differentiation.title: Design your literary life
differentiation.activity: Students design a four-week independent reading and writing plan. They select texts representing personal interest and academic challenge, establish measurable goals, choose strategies, and create an original writing project connected to their reading. Students participate in peer conferences, maintain a process log, and curate a final portfolio demonstrating choices, growth, and reflection.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional planning template, individual conferences, model portfolio, peer critique.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate purposeful text selection, monitored and revised goals, strategic reading and writing decisions, meaningful community participation, and evidence of growing independence.
differentiation.materials: Library collection or digital reading platform; reading log; writing portfolio; conference guide.

questions.prompt: Which reading goal is most useful for monitoring progress and making adjustments?
options: Become a better reader.
Read more books than everyone else.
Read independently for 20 minutes on four days each week, record questions, and review progress after two weeks.
Never encounter an unfamiliar word.
questions.answer: Read independently for 20 minutes on four days each week, record questions, and review progress after two weeks.
questions.rationale: The goal identifies specific actions and includes an opportunity to monitor and revise progress.

questions.prompt: During a peer writing workshop, which response best supports a productive community of writers?
options: This is bad. Start over.
I liked it.
Your opening establishes the conflict clearly. I wanted more detail about the character's decision in the third paragraph.
I would write the entire story differently.
questions.answer: Your opening establishes the conflict clearly. I wanted more detail about the character's decision in the third paragraph.
questions.rationale: The feedback is specific, respectful, and actionable while preserving the writer's ownership of the work.

questions.prompt: Describe a reading or writing preference you have developed. Identify a specific genre, topic, technique, or mode that appeals to you and explain why. Then identify one unfamiliar type of text that could help you grow.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies a specific preference, supports it with an authentic example or explanation, and proposes a meaningful opportunity to expand the student's reading or writing repertoire.
questions.rationale: Assesses students' ability to articulate preferences while considering opportunities for growth.

questions.prompt: Think of a reading or writing task that challenged you. Describe the difficulty, the strategy you selected, whether it helped, and what you would do independently next time.
questions.answer: A strong response accurately describes the challenge, identifies a relevant strategy, evaluates its effectiveness, and proposes a reasonable next step.
questions.rationale: Assesses awareness and purposeful use of reading and writing strategies as well as developing autonomy.

questions.prompt: Create a four-week reader and writer identity portfolio. Include a reading goal, a writing goal, at least two purposeful text selections, records of reading and writing strategies, one original writing sample, evidence of participation in a reading or writing community, and a final reflection explaining how your goals, preferences, strategies, or independence changed.
questions.answer: Evaluate the specificity and revision of goals, reasoning behind text choices, evidence of strategy use, quality of participation and feedback, thoughtful reflection, and demonstration of increasingly independent decisions. Do not grade personal interests, reading speed, or the quantity of books alone.
questions.rationale: Provides authentic evidence of all six expectations through sustained practice, participation, and reflection.

evidence: A personal and academic reading and writing goal-setting document with progress updates.
A reading and writing interest inventory supported by specific examples.
A reading selection record explaining personal interest and academic relevance.
A strategy reflection showing how comprehension or composition approaches were selected and evaluated.
A literature-circle or writing-workshop participation record.
Peer feedback and evidence of the student's response to that feedback.
A portfolio of independently selected reading and writing work.
A reflective statement documenting growth in confidence, choice, strategy use, or autonomy.
instruction: Establish a classroom culture in which students can describe themselves as developing readers and writers without being labeled as inherently strong or weak.
Use brief reading and writing inventories to learn about students' interests, experiences, and goals.
Model specific, actionable goals and provide scheduled opportunities for monitoring and revision.
Offer meaningful choices among texts that combine student interests with appropriate academic challenge.
Include varied genres, formats, voices, and modes so students can discover new interests.
Teach comprehension and composition strategies explicitly, then help students decide when each strategy is useful.
Build regular independent reading and writing opportunities into instruction.
Use short individual conferences to support goal-setting, text selection, and reflection.
Establish shared norms for respectful discussion, active listening, and constructive feedback.
Teach students how to respond to feedback thoughtfully rather than requiring them to accept every suggestion.
Use portfolios and reflective writing to document growth over time.
Gradually transfer responsibility for text selection, strategy use, and writing decisions to students.
Recognize that reading and writing identities are influenced by access, language background, culture, previous experiences, and opportunities.
Assess observable decisions, reflection, strategy use, and participation rather than students' private preferences or self-reported enjoyment.
watchFor: Reducing reader and writer identity to a one-time interest survey.
Assuming that students who dislike assigned reading dislike all reading.
Treating a preferred genre or format as evidence of limited ability.
Equating reading volume or speed with a student's value or identity as a reader.
Setting goals without providing opportunities to monitor or revise them.
Offering student choice without sufficient access to varied, appropriate texts.
Requiring students to share private personal experiences in order to demonstrate identity development.
Teaching reading and writing strategies as fixed procedures rather than flexible tools.
Assuming students become independent simply because they work alone.
Using literature circles without explicitly teaching discussion norms and listening skills.
Allowing peer feedback to become vague praise, unsupported criticism, or rewriting another student's work.
Grading students on whether they claim to enjoy reading or writing.
Treating independence as the absence of teacher support rather than the development of informed decision-making.
Overemphasizing logs, point systems, or compliance at the expense of meaningful reading and writing.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. This practice standard is best supported through varied student-selected and shared texts rather than a single required literary work. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level scores. Reading and writing preferences are personal and evolving; assessment should focus on reflection, strategy use, participation, and growth rather than requiring particular interests or attitudes.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can read, write, speak, and listen for different purposes: to tell stories, learn, explain, analyze ideas, solve problems, and influence decisions. I can connect what I learn from texts to other texts and to the world around me.
know: People engage with texts for different purposes, including storytelling, learning, explaining, evaluating, and influencing decisions.
Texts include written, spoken, visual, digital, and multimodal communications.
A single text may serve several purposes at once.
Narrative texts can communicate real or imagined experiences.
Informational texts can build knowledge and support informed decisions.
Explanatory texts can clarify concepts, processes, and relationships.
Analytical and evaluative texts examine ideas, evidence, and significance.
Persuasive and problem-solving texts can propose actions and influence decisions.
Readers and writers make connections within a text, between texts, and beyond texts.
Audience, purpose, and context influence how people interpret and construct texts.
Dialogue involves exchanging ideas as both a communicator and an audience member.
Effective communication requires selecting forms and strategies suited to a specific task.
understand: Purpose shapes the way people approach, interpret, and create texts.
Reading and writing are active ways of developing knowledge rather than merely receiving or recording information.
Stories can communicate experiences and perspectives that help audiences understand human situations.
Explanation supports learning by making complex ideas and processes more understandable.
Analysis and evaluation help people examine assumptions, evidence, and competing interpretations.
Texts can support practical problem-solving and responsible decision-making.
Connections among texts and real-world experiences deepen understanding.
Effective communicators move flexibly among different purposes and modes of communication.
Interpretation and construction are connected processes: reading informs writing, and writing can deepen reading.
do: Interpret stories and construct narrative texts that communicate real or imagined experiences (9.P.EICC.2.a).
Use texts to acquire knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, and communicate information or ideas (9.P.EICC.2.b).
Interpret explanations and construct texts that clarify concepts, procedures, or processes (9.P.EICC.2.c).
Analyze and evaluate texts and ideas, then communicate supported interpretations and judgments (9.P.EICC.2.d).
Interpret texts addressing problems or decisions and construct texts proposing solutions or influencing decisions (9.P.EICC.2.e).
Identify the primary and secondary purposes of texts encountered in different contexts (9.P.EICC.2.a–e).
Make purposeful connections within, between, and beyond texts when developing or communicating ideas (9.P.EICC.2.a–e).
Adapt communication choices to audience, task, context, and intended outcome (9.P.EICC.2.a–e).
targets: I can explain why a text was created and what its audience might gain from it.
I can interpret and create stories that communicate meaningful experiences.
I can use texts to answer questions and develop knowledge.
I can explain a concept or process clearly to a particular audience.
I can analyze and evaluate ideas using relevant evidence.
I can use information from texts to make or recommend informed decisions.
I can create a text that proposes a solution to a real or imagined problem.
I can connect ideas within one text, across multiple texts, and to broader situations.
I can explain how my communication choices support my purpose.

vocabulary.definition: The reason a person interprets or creates a text.
vocabulary.example: A student reads an article to understand an issue and writes a proposal to recommend a solution.

vocabulary.definition: The process of constructing meaning from a text using evidence, context, and reasoning.
vocabulary.example: A reader interprets a character's decision by examining the character's actions and circumstances.

vocabulary.definition: The process of creating a text to communicate meaning for a particular audience and purpose.
vocabulary.example: A student constructs an explanatory presentation about a scientific process.

vocabulary.definition: A text that tells or incorporates a story involving experiences, events, or characters.
vocabulary.example: A personal narrative recounts an experience that changed the writer's perspective.

vocabulary.definition: Communication intended to explain or inform.
vocabulary.example: An article explains how a city's water treatment system operates.

vocabulary.definition: Close examination of components and relationships to develop understanding.
vocabulary.example: An essay analyzes how a writer uses contrasting perspectives.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned judgment about the quality, effectiveness, significance, or value of something.
vocabulary.example: A student evaluates whether a proposed school policy addresses the identified problem.

vocabulary.definition: The integration of information or ideas from multiple sources into a coherent understanding.
vocabulary.example: A researcher combines findings from several articles to explain a community issue.

vocabulary.definition: A meaningful relationship identified between two or more texts.
vocabulary.example: A student compares how a short story and an editorial portray responsibility.

vocabulary.definition: A relationship between ideas in a text and broader historical, social, scientific, or contemporary circumstances.
vocabulary.example: A reader connects a novel's treatment of censorship to debates about access to information.

vocabulary.definition: The process of identifying a problem, examining relevant information, and developing or evaluating possible responses.
vocabulary.example: Students research food waste and propose changes to cafeteria procedures.

vocabulary.definition: A choice made after considering relevant evidence, consequences, and alternatives.
vocabulary.example: A committee reviews survey results and cost estimates before recommending a new program.

vocabulary.definition: A statement encouraging an audience to take a particular step.
vocabulary.example: A proposal asks school leaders to establish a student-led recycling initiative.

suggestedTexts.title: Thank You, M'am

suggestedTexts.access: Licensed anthology or authorized text.

suggestedTexts.title: The Danger of a Single Story

suggestedTexts.interestHook: How the stories people encounter influence their understanding of others
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the speaker move from telling personal stories to explaining a broader social idea?

suggestedTexts.interestHook: An outrageous proposal exposes the failures of supposedly practical reasoning
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Why is it essential to distinguish the proposal's literal content from the author's satirical purpose?

suggestedTexts.author: Ray Bradbury

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the novel use imagined events to encourage readers to evaluate real-world ideas?

suggestedTexts.author: Rebecca Skloot

suggestedTexts.access: Licensed book or authorized excerpt.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A family's experience raises important questions about medical research
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the writer combine storytelling and scientific information to help readers evaluate an ethical issue?

suggestedTexts.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
suggestedTexts.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
suggestedTexts.purpose: Study how explanation, analysis, and argument respond to a specific audience and seek to influence judgment.
suggestedTexts.access: Use an authorized text or licensed excerpt.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A response written from jail that addresses criticism and argues for social change
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the writer combine explanation, ethical reasoning, and direct response to an audience?

suggestedTexts.title: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
suggestedTexts.author: William Kamkwamba and Bryan Mealer
suggestedTexts.purpose: Explore how reading and acquired knowledge can support practical problem-solving and how narrative communicates that process.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed book or authorized excerpt; a young readers edition is available.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A teenager uses books and ingenuity to develop a practical invention
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the author's experience demonstrate connections among learning from texts, explaining ideas, and solving problems?

differentiation.title: Five reasons we use texts
differentiation.activity: Students examine five short, teacher-created texts: a narrative, an informational notice, a how-to explanation, an evaluation, and a proposal. They identify each text's primary purpose, highlight evidence supporting their decision, and compose a short example of one selected purpose.
differentiation.scaffolds: Purpose reference chart, short accessible examples, color-coded annotations, sentence frames, teacher modeling.
differentiation.success: Identify the primary purpose of at least four texts, support two classifications with evidence, and create a short text that fulfills an identified purpose.
differentiation.materials: Five short sample texts; purpose chart; annotation tools.

differentiation.title: One topic, three purposes
differentiation.activity: Students select a familiar school or community topic, such as school lunch, transportation, or recreational spaces. They read two short texts presenting relevant information. They then create three distinct communications: a brief narrative illustrating an experience, an explanation of the issue, and a recommendation supported by evidence. Students annotate how purpose influenced their choices.
differentiation.scaffolds: Text selection guide, three-purpose planning organizer, models of each form, peer feedback.
differentiation.success: Produce three clearly differentiated texts, use relevant information accurately, and explain at least three purposeful communication choices.
differentiation.materials: Two informational texts; planning organizer; writing document.

differentiation.title: From inquiry to impact
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a genuine school or community problem using multiple credible texts. They synthesize findings, evaluate proposed solutions, and create a communication package for a defined audience: a short explanatory brief, an evidence-based recommendation, and a narrative or visual element illustrating the human implications of the issue. Students present the package and reflect on the strengths and limitations of their evidence.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional inquiry template, source evaluation checklist, audience planning guide, conferencing.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate accurate understanding, meaningful connections across sources, reasoned evaluation of alternatives, and a persuasive recommendation appropriate to the audience.
differentiation.materials: Credible sources; research organizer; presentation or publishing tools; evaluation rubric.

questions.prompt: A student reads several articles about local water quality and uses the findings to recommend a new testing procedure. Which purpose is most directly demonstrated?
options: Sharing an imagined experience
Solving a problem or influencing a decision
Recounting events for entertainment
Describing a character's motivation
questions.answer: Solving a problem or influencing a decision
questions.rationale: The student interprets information and constructs a recommendation intended to address a practical problem.

questions.prompt: Which task most directly demonstrates using texts to explain and learn a process?
options: Reading a procedural article and creating an illustrated guide that accurately explains its steps
Reading a short story and identifying the protagonist
Listing the titles of five favorite books
Memorizing the publication dates of several novels
questions.answer: Reading a procedural article and creating an illustrated guide that accurately explains its steps
questions.rationale: The task requires both interpretation and construction of explanatory texts focused on a process.

questions.prompt: A writer publishes a personal story about struggling to access public transportation, followed by factual information about transportation options. Explain two different purposes the combined text could serve.
questions.answer: The personal story may communicate an experience and help readers understand its human significance. The factual information may build knowledge, clarify the issue, or support informed decisions. A strong response explains how the two purposes reinforce one another.
questions.rationale: Assesses recognition of overlapping purposes within a single text.

questions.prompt: Read two short texts that address the same issue but reach different conclusions. Identify one point of agreement, one point of disagreement, and the evidence each author uses. Explain which conclusion is better supported and why.
questions.answer: A strong response accurately identifies the texts' positions, distinguishes agreement from disagreement, evaluates relevant evidence, and supports a reasoned judgment without relying solely on personal preference.
questions.rationale: Assesses interpretation and construction of analysis and evaluation, including connections between texts.

questions.prompt: Choose a school or community issue. Read at least three relevant texts representing different kinds of information or perspectives. Create a communication portfolio containing: a 150–200-word narrative illustrating an experience connected to the issue; a 200-word explanation of its causes, processes, or background; a 250-word analysis evaluating relevant evidence or possible responses; and a 200-word proposal recommending an informed action. Conclude with a reflection explaining how the texts informed your thinking and how your purpose changed across the four pieces.
questions.answer: Evaluate the accurate interpretation of sources, effectiveness of storytelling, clarity of explanation, quality of analysis, reasoning behind the proposed action, purposeful connections among texts, and the student's ability to adapt communication to different purposes.
questions.rationale: Integrates all five expectations through a coherent sequence of interpretation and construction tasks.

evidence: An annotated collection of texts identifying primary and secondary communicative purposes.
An original narrative communicating a real or imagined experience.
A knowledge-building response synthesizing information from a text.
An explanation of a concept or process for a defined audience.
An analytical or evaluative response supported by textual evidence.
A proposal addressing a problem or recommending a decision.
A comparative organizer documenting connections within, between, and beyond texts.
A reflection explaining how audience and purpose influenced choices during composition.
instruction: Introduce the standard by asking students what they want to accomplish when they read, write, speak, or listen.
Teach the five expectations as overlapping communicative purposes rather than rigid, mutually exclusive genres.
Use authentic examples showing how a single text may tell a story, explain an idea, and influence an audience.
Model the distinction between identifying a text's topic and identifying its purpose.
Provide paired interpretation and construction activities so students read with a purpose and then create something meaningful.
Use narrative as a means of communicating experience without assuming that every narrative must be autobiographical.
Teach students to distinguish explaining information from analyzing or evaluating its significance.
Provide real or realistic decision-making contexts that require students to consider evidence and alternatives.
Build text-to-text connections through comparison, synthesis, and discussion.
Extend text-to-world connections through relevant historical, scientific, cultural, or community contexts.
Offer varied modes of communication, including written, spoken, visual, and multimodal texts when appropriate.
Teach students to identify a specific audience and intended outcome before composing.
Use reflection prompts asking students how their purpose shaped selection, organization, evidence, and language.
Assess how successfully a text fulfills its purpose, not merely whether it follows a familiar format.
watchFor: Treating the five expectations as five fixed writing genres rather than purposes that can overlap.
Confusing the topic of a text with the reason it was created.
Assuming all stories exist only to entertain.
Equating knowledge-building with copying or listing facts.
Confusing explanation with unsupported opinion.
Treating analysis as summary without examination of relationships or significance.
Treating evaluation as personal preference without criteria or evidence.
Asking students to solve problems without supplying sufficient information or a realistic decision-making context.
Assuming that a persuasive text is effective simply because it expresses a strong opinion.
Making superficial text-to-world connections that do not deepen understanding.
Expecting students to construct effective texts without first examining examples.
Ignoring how audience and purpose affect the choice of form, detail, evidence, and language.
Requiring personal disclosure when an imagined narrative could demonstrate the same expectation.
Grading students primarily on whether they advocate a preferred solution rather than on the quality of their reasoning.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm text access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level scores. Because this practice standard addresses multiple purposes and text types, teachers should supplement literary selections with authentic informational, explanatory, analytical, and problem-solving texts. Students should be assessed on the quality of interpretation and construction, not on agreement with a particular position.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can investigate the historical, cultural, geographic, and social circumstances surrounding a text. I can explain how those circumstances influence an author's choices, an audience's response, and the way I interpret or create texts.
know: Context includes circumstances that surround the creation, circulation, interpretation, and reception of a text.
Historical context includes events, conditions, and ideas associated with a particular time period.
Geographic context includes locations and physical environments that may influence experiences and perspectives.
Cultural context includes traditions, values, languages, practices, and shared experiences that may influence communication.
Social and political circumstances can influence the issues writers address and the choices available to them.
Contemporary events can shape both the creation of new texts and the interpretation of older ones.
Authors and audiences may possess different knowledge, assumptions, experiences, and expectations.
Primary sources and credible secondary sources can provide useful contextual information.
Prior knowledge and discussion can generate contextual questions, but claims should be checked against reliable evidence.
Not every contextual detail is equally relevant to understanding a particular text.
Context can inform interpretation without determining a single correct meaning.
Writers make decisions about language, examples, references, and explanation based partly on the circumstances of their intended audiences.
understand: Texts emerge from particular circumstances rather than existing in isolation.
Relevant contextual knowledge can clarify references, conflicts, assumptions, and choices that readers might otherwise misunderstand.
Historical and cultural circumstances can influence an author's purposes without fully explaining every artistic or rhetorical decision.
Audiences from different times, places, and communities may interpret the same text differently.
Contextual investigation requires selecting information that meaningfully contributes to an interpretation.
Evidence from the text and evidence about its context should work together.
Writers can anticipate audience knowledge and provide necessary context to make their communications more effective.
Responsible contextual analysis avoids reducing individuals or communities to stereotypes.
New contextual knowledge may complicate or change an initial interpretation.
do: Activate relevant prior knowledge and identify questions about a text's circumstances (9.P.ST.1.a).
Use formal or informal research and discussion to investigate relevant historical, geographic, cultural, or contemporary context (9.P.ST.1.a).
Distinguish contextual information that meaningfully supports interpretation from background details that are merely interesting (9.P.ST.1.a).
Explain how context may influence an author's purpose or intended audience (9.P.ST.1.b).
Consider how different audiences' circumstances and expectations may influence their purposes for engaging with a text (9.P.ST.1.b).
Analyze relationships between context and an author's choices of subject, language, structure, examples, or emphasis (9.P.ST.1.c).
Explore how different audiences may respond to the same text because of differences in contextual knowledge or experience (9.P.ST.1.c).
Use contextual knowledge when constructing texts, including decisions about what background information an audience needs (9.P.ST.1.a–c).
Support contextual interpretations with relevant evidence from texts and credible contextual sources (9.P.ST.1.a–c).
targets: I can identify which aspects of context are important to understanding a text.
I can investigate a contextual question using credible sources or informed discussion.
I can explain how an event, location, or cultural circumstance relates to a text.
I can connect contextual information to a specific passage or authorial choice.
I can explain how context may influence an author's purpose.
I can compare how audiences from different circumstances might respond to a text.
I can revise my interpretation when new contextual evidence becomes available.
I can provide appropriate background information when writing for a particular audience.
I can distinguish evidence-based contextual analysis from unsupported assumptions.

vocabulary.definition: The circumstances surrounding the creation, content, interpretation, or reception of a text.
vocabulary.example: Understanding the conditions of the Great Depression may illuminate references in a novel set during that period.

vocabulary.definition: The events, conditions, beliefs, and circumstances associated with a particular period.
vocabulary.example: The American Civil War provides important context for interpreting the Gettysburg Address.

vocabulary.definition: The practices, values, languages, traditions, and experiences relevant to a text or its audience.
vocabulary.example: Knowledge of cultural traditions can help readers understand references in a memoir.

vocabulary.definition: The physical location and environmental circumstances relevant to a text.
vocabulary.example: A coastal community's geography may influence the conflicts described in a story.

vocabulary.definition: The social structures, relationships, institutions, and expectations relevant to communication.
vocabulary.example: Social expectations about gender may help explain a character's limited choices.

vocabulary.definition: The governmental conditions, power relationships, policies, and public debates relevant to a text.
vocabulary.example: A speech advocating voting rights responds to a particular political situation.

vocabulary.definition: Events occurring during a particular period, especially those relevant to the creation or interpretation of a text.
vocabulary.example: A recent natural disaster may shape the urgency of a community announcement.

vocabulary.definition: Original evidence or firsthand material from the period, event, or subject being investigated.
vocabulary.example: A contemporary newspaper article can provide evidence about how an event was reported at the time.

vocabulary.definition: A source that analyzes, interprets, or explains information drawn from other evidence.
vocabulary.example: A historian's scholarly article analyzes the circumstances surrounding a historical speech.

vocabulary.definition: The people a text was originally designed to reach.
vocabulary.example: A public letter may address named critics while also appealing to a wider readership.

vocabulary.definition: The ways audiences respond to or interpret a text.
vocabulary.example: A novel may receive different responses when it is published and when it is studied decades later.

vocabulary.definition: A decision an author makes about a text's content, form, language, or presentation.
vocabulary.example: A writer includes a familiar historical reference to establish common ground with an audience.

vocabulary.definition: The tendency to interpret the past primarily through present-day assumptions or values without adequately considering historical circumstances.
vocabulary.example: A reader overlooks the limitations of a historical character's circumstances when judging every choice solely by modern expectations.

suggestedTexts.title: A Raisin in the Sun
suggestedTexts.author: Lorraine Hansberry
suggestedTexts.purpose: Explore how housing discrimination, family expectations, and the social circumstances of mid-twentieth-century Chicago shape the play's conflicts.

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does historical knowledge about housing discrimination deepen an interpretation of the family's decisions?

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does understanding the novel's cultural and historical contexts help readers avoid interpreting its characters through unsupported assumptions?

suggestedTexts.title: The Diary of a Young Girl
suggestedTexts.author: Anne Frank
suggestedTexts.context: Amsterdam · Nazi occupation of the Netherlands · 1942–1944

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What historical information is necessary to understand the diary's circumstances without reducing the writer to a symbol rather than an individual?

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How might audiences with different experiences or ethical frameworks respond to the same fictional arrangement?

suggestedTexts.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
suggestedTexts.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how the immediate circumstances of King's imprisonment and the criticism to which he responds shape the letter's audience, purpose, and reasoning.
suggestedTexts.access: Use an authorized text or licensed excerpt.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A public argument written in response to criticism during a major civil rights campaign
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does identifying the letter's immediate audience and circumstances clarify the author's rhetorical decisions?

differentiation.title: Three clues to context
differentiation.activity: Students read a short literary passage and examine three teacher-selected contextual sources: a brief timeline, an image or map, and a short explanatory paragraph. They identify which source provides the most relevant information for understanding a specific textual detail. Students then explain the connection using a sentence frame.
differentiation.scaffolds: Short accessible passage, curated sources, visual timeline, color-coded evidence, modeled explanation.
differentiation.success: Identify two relevant contextual facts and accurately connect each to a detail in the text.
differentiation.materials: Literary excerpt; timeline; map or image; short contextual source; response organizer.

differentiation.title: Read it twice
differentiation.activity: Students read 'The Story of an Hour' without extensive historical introduction and record an initial interpretation. They then investigate a small collection of credible sources about the period's social expectations. After rereading, they revise or complicate their interpretation, citing both textual and contextual evidence.
differentiation.scaffolds: Contextual source packet, before-and-after organizer, teacher model distinguishing evidence from inference, partner discussion.
differentiation.success: Explain at least two meaningful connections between context and textual choices and describe how contextual evidence influenced an interpretation.
differentiation.materials: Short story; credible historical sources; comparative interpretation organizer.

differentiation.title: One text, multiple audiences
differentiation.activity: Students investigate the original circumstances and reception of a historical speech, literary work, or public argument. They identify its intended audience and research at least one later audience or interpretive context. Students compose a comparative analysis explaining how circumstances may influence purpose, authorial choices, and audience responses. They then write a short introduction designed to provide essential context to a contemporary reader.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional source evaluation guide, contextual research planner, analytical writing model, individual conference.
differentiation.success: Use credible evidence to explain relevant context, distinguish supported conclusions from speculation, compare audience responses, and provide an effective contextual introduction.
differentiation.materials: Selected text; primary and secondary sources; research organizer; writing document.

questions.prompt: A student is studying the Gettysburg Address. Which information would be most directly relevant to interpreting the speech's immediate purpose?
options: The history of printing technology in the eighteenth century
The Civil War and the dedication ceremony at which Lincoln delivered the speech
The architectural design of the modern Lincoln Memorial
The number of American presidents who served after Lincoln
questions.answer: The Civil War and the dedication ceremony at which Lincoln delivered the speech
questions.rationale: The speech's historical circumstances and occasion directly inform its purpose and intended audience.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the relationship between context and interpretation?
options: Context always determines one correct interpretation of a text.
Context is useful only when a text contains unfamiliar vocabulary.
Relevant context can deepen or complicate an interpretation when connected to textual evidence.
Modern readers should ignore historical circumstances when evaluating older texts.
questions.answer: Relevant context can deepen or complicate an interpretation when connected to textual evidence.
questions.rationale: Context informs interpretation but does not replace close reading or eliminate reasonable differences among readers.

questions.prompt: A novel was published during a period of major social change. Explain how researching that period might help you understand the author's choices. Identify one type of contextual source you would consult.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies a specific possible relationship between social circumstances and an author's subject, language, characterization, or purpose. It proposes an appropriate contextual source and avoids claiming that historical circumstances automatically explain the author's intentions.
questions.rationale: Assesses selection of relevant context and reasoning about its relationship to authorial decisions.

questions.prompt: A speech delivered to a local community during a crisis is republished decades later for students studying history. Explain how the purposes and responses of the original audience and the later student audience might differ.
questions.answer: The original audience may have sought guidance, reassurance, or immediate action, while the later audience may seek historical understanding or rhetorical analysis. A strong response connects these possibilities to the audiences' circumstances and recognizes that individual responses can vary.
questions.rationale: Assesses consideration of how context influences audience purposes and responses.

questions.prompt: Select a literary, historical, or rhetorical text for which relevant contextual sources are available. Investigate at least three contextual factors, such as time period, location, cultural circumstances, or contemporary events. Write a 350–500-word analysis explaining which factors are most relevant, how they may have influenced the author's purpose and decisions, and how audiences in different circumstances might respond. Support the analysis with textual evidence and credible contextual sources. Then compose a 150-word introduction that provides essential context for a new audience.
questions.answer: Evaluate the relevance and accuracy of contextual research, the distinction between evidence and inference, the explanation of relationships among context, purpose, authorial choices, and audience responses, and the effectiveness of the contextual introduction.
questions.rationale: Integrates contextual investigation, interpretation of author and audience purposes, and purposeful construction for a defined audience.

evidence: A contextual inquiry chart identifying relevant questions and credible sources.
An annotated text connecting contextual information to specific passages.
A before-and-after interpretation showing how research affected a student's understanding.
A short analysis explaining the relationship between context and an author's purpose.
A comparison of possible audience responses across different historical or cultural circumstances.
A contextual introduction written for a contemporary audience.
A research-supported interpretation that distinguishes textual evidence, contextual evidence, and inference.
A reflection explaining which contextual details were most useful and why.
instruction: Begin with the text and identify contextual questions that arise naturally from reading.
Teach students to prioritize relevant context rather than collecting large quantities of disconnected background information.
Use primary and credible secondary sources to investigate historical, cultural, geographic, and contemporary circumstances.
Model how to distinguish established contextual facts from plausible but unverified claims about authorial intention.
Pair contextual research with close reading so students connect background knowledge to specific textual details.
Use maps, timelines, images, historical documents, and short scholarly explanations as appropriate.
Encourage students to revise initial interpretations when new evidence changes their understanding.
Examine how intended audiences and later audiences may bring different knowledge and expectations to a text.
Avoid presenting cultures, historical periods, or communities as internally uniform.
Teach students to distinguish the setting of a fictional work from the circumstances of its composition and publication.
Provide opportunities to write contextual introductions for audiences unfamiliar with a topic.
Use discussion to test competing contextual interpretations against available evidence.
Assess the quality of contextual reasoning rather than the quantity of historical facts memorized.
Include contemporary texts so students can examine how current events and audience circumstances influence communication.
watchFor: Treating context as an introductory history lecture disconnected from the text.
Assuming every historical fact about an author or period is relevant.
Replacing close reading with biographical or historical summary.
Claiming certainty about an author's private intentions without adequate evidence.
Assuming all members of a historical or cultural group shared the same beliefs.
Using stereotypes as substitutes for cultural research.
Confusing a fictional story's setting with the time and place in which it was written.
Assuming a text's original audience responded in only one way.
Treating a contemporary audience's interpretation as necessarily superior to earlier interpretations.
Ignoring differences among primary sources, secondary analysis, and unsupported online commentary.
Presenting contextual speculation as established fact.
Assuming that understanding historical circumstances requires agreeing with the beliefs or actions represented.
Allowing contextual research to become so extensive that students never return to interpretation or composition.
Using historical background as a substitute for supporting claims with textual evidence.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Historical and cultural context should be researched using credible sources and connected to specific textual evidence. Context can inform interpretation without proving a single authorial intention or audience response.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can explain how writers make choices for particular audiences and purposes. I can develop a clear perspective and choose information, language, structure, and design that help my own writing accomplish its purpose.
know: An author is the creator of a text, and an audience is the group of people who receive or engage with it.
Purpose refers to what an author seeks to accomplish through a text.
Context includes circumstances surrounding the creation, distribution, and reception of a text.
Point of view or perspective reflects a particular position, understanding, or way of approaching a subject.
Authors may seek to inform, explain, entertain, persuade, challenge assumptions, inspire action, or accomplish several purposes simultaneously.
The same subject may require different information, language, and presentation when addressed to different audiences.
Writers select and emphasize information according to its relevance to their purposes and audiences.
Text design includes organizational and visual choices that influence accessibility and meaning.
Diction, sentence structure, tone, and rhetorical techniques influence how an audience experiences a text.
Authors may anticipate audience questions, concerns, expectations, and prior knowledge.
The effectiveness of a text can be evaluated in relation to its intended purpose and audience.
A text may affect an audience differently from what its author intended.
understand: Authors make purposeful choices about what to communicate and how to communicate it.
Audience awareness requires more than identifying demographic characteristics; it involves considering readers' needs, knowledge, expectations, and circumstances.
A clear perspective helps organize and unify a text's decisions.
Communication strategies that work for one audience or purpose may be ineffective for another.
Effective text design helps audiences locate, understand, and use information.
Word choice and sentence structure can strengthen clarity, credibility, emotional impact, or engagement.
Evaluating a text's effectiveness requires evidence about its features and intended outcomes.
Writers improve their work by anticipating how audiences may interpret and respond to their choices.
Purpose, audience, perspective, and context interact throughout interpretation and composition.
do: Identify and analyze the author, intended audience, context, and purpose of a text (9.P.ST.2.a).
Evaluate how effectively a text's content and techniques accomplish its apparent purpose for its intended audience (9.P.ST.2.a).
Establish a clear purpose and intended audience before constructing a text (9.P.ST.2.a).
Analyze how an author's point of view or unique perspective influences a text (9.P.ST.2.b).
Develop and maintain a clear perspective appropriate to a chosen audience and purpose (9.P.ST.2.b).
Analyze which information and ideas an author emphasizes or omits and explain the possible effects of those decisions (9.P.ST.2.c).
Evaluate how text design, diction, syntax, and craft techniques serve a particular audience (9.P.ST.2.c).
Select relevant information, accessible design, effective language, and appropriate craft techniques when composing (9.P.ST.2.c).
Revise a text after evaluating whether its choices support the intended audience, perspective, and purpose (9.P.ST.2.a–c).
targets: I can identify an author's intended audience and explain my reasoning.
I can determine a text's primary purpose and identify evidence supporting that interpretation.
I can evaluate whether a text achieves its purpose.
I can explain how a writer's perspective influences the presentation of ideas.
I can establish a clear perspective in my own writing.
I can explain why a writer highlights particular information.
I can evaluate whether a text's organization and design are accessible to its audience.

I can revise a text to improve its effectiveness for a different audience.

vocabulary.definition: The person or group responsible for creating a text.

vocabulary.definition: The people a text is designed primarily to reach.
vocabulary.example: A course-selection guide addresses students preparing to choose classes.

vocabulary.definition: The outcome or effect an author seeks to accomplish.
vocabulary.example: A public-service announcement encourages residents to prepare for severe weather.

vocabulary.definition: The circumstances influencing a text's creation, content, distribution, or interpretation.
vocabulary.example: A community announcement responds to a recent change in transportation services.

vocabulary.definition: A particular way of understanding or approaching a subject.
vocabulary.example: A student athlete and a school administrator may emphasize different concerns when discussing a proposed schedule.

vocabulary.definition: A position or standpoint from which a subject is presented.
vocabulary.example: An editorial presents the writer's position on a proposed policy.

vocabulary.definition: The interaction among communicator, audience, purpose, subject, and circumstances.
vocabulary.example: A principal addresses families after an unexpected school closure.

vocabulary.definition: A decision about language, content, organization, or technique intended to influence communication.
vocabulary.example: A speaker begins with a personal story to establish a connection with listeners.

vocabulary.definition: An author's purposeful selection of words.
vocabulary.example: A science writer explains a technical term before using it repeatedly.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses in sentences.
vocabulary.example: A writer uses a short sentence to emphasize an important warning.

vocabulary.definition: The organizational, visual, and structural arrangement of a text.
vocabulary.example: A guide uses descriptive headings, readable spacing, and clearly labeled steps.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which people can perceive, navigate, understand, and use a text.
vocabulary.example: An online guide provides descriptive headings, meaningful link text, and readable formatting.

vocabulary.definition: Special attention given to particular information or ideas.
vocabulary.example: A proposal places its most important recommendation near the beginning.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which a text accomplishes its intended purpose for an audience.
vocabulary.example: A set of instructions is effective when its intended readers can follow the process accurately.

differentiation.title: Who is this for?
differentiation.activity: Students examine three short communications about the same topic: a message to students, a formal report for administrators, and a family-facing announcement. They identify each text's likely audience and purpose, highlight clues in word choice and information, and revise one sentence for a different audience.
differentiation.scaffolds: Audience cards, color-coded texts, purpose chart, teacher modeling, sentence frames.
differentiation.success: Correctly identify the intended audiences of three texts, support two choices with textual evidence, and make one purposeful audience-based revision.
differentiation.materials: Three teacher-created communications; audience and purpose organizer; revision worksheet.

differentiation.title: The audience shift
differentiation.activity: Students read a short public argument and annotate its purpose, perspective, supporting information, diction, and organizational choices. They then rewrite a 150-word portion for a substantially different audience while preserving the central idea. Students explain four changes and evaluate whether their revision better serves the new audience.
differentiation.scaffolds: Rhetorical analysis organizer, audience profiles, model adaptation, peer feedback.
differentiation.success: Identify the original text's purpose and perspective, make at least four justified revisions, and explain their effects on the new audience.
differentiation.materials: Public argument excerpt; audience profiles; writing document; comparison chart.

differentiation.title: Design for a real audience
differentiation.activity: Students identify an authentic school communication problem, such as confusing course-selection instructions, an unclear club announcement, or an inaccessible event guide. They investigate the needs of the intended audience, evaluate an existing communication, and create an improved version. Their final product includes a clear perspective and purpose, purposeful information selection, accessible design, appropriate language, and a written rationale. Where practical, students test the revision with representative users.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional audience research protocol, accessibility checklist, communication audit template, teacher conference.
differentiation.success: Produce an audience-centered communication with evidence-based design decisions and a clear explanation of how those decisions improve effectiveness.
differentiation.materials: Existing communication sample; audience analysis worksheet; publishing tools; evaluation rubric.

questions.prompt: A school publishes instructions for incoming ninth-grade students selecting their first high school courses. Which design decision best serves the intended audience?
options: Use unexplained abbreviations because school employees already know them.
Present every district policy in one uninterrupted paragraph.
Organize instructions into clearly labeled steps and explain unfamiliar terms.
Place the most important deadlines in an unrelated document without a link.
questions.answer: Organize instructions into clearly labeled steps and explain unfamiliar terms.
questions.rationale: The design anticipates the audience's limited prior knowledge and makes the required information easier to understand and use.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful when evaluating whether an author has achieved a text's purpose?
options: Does the text contain at least five paragraphs?
Would every possible reader agree with the author?
How do the text's evidence, language, and design support its intended outcome for its audience?
Does the author use the longest words available?
questions.answer: How do the text's evidence, language, and design support its intended outcome for its audience?
questions.rationale: Evaluating effectiveness requires examining the relationship among purpose, audience, and the author's choices.

questions.prompt: Two writers discuss the same proposed school policy. One is a student affected by the policy, and the other is an administrator responsible for implementing it. Explain how their perspectives might influence which information they emphasize. Avoid assuming that either perspective is automatically more accurate.
questions.answer: A strong response explains that a student may emphasize everyday experiences and consequences, while an administrator may emphasize implementation, resources, or institutional responsibilities. The response recognizes that individual authors can differ and that claims still require evidence.
questions.rationale: Assesses understanding of how authorial perspective can shape content and emphasis.

questions.prompt: Revise this announcement for students who have never attended a high school club meeting: 'All interested parties should report to the designated venue for organizational proceedings.' Explain how your revision better serves the audience.
questions.answer: One appropriate revision is: 'Interested in joining the club? Come to our first meeting in Room 214 on Thursday after school.' The revision uses familiar language and a welcoming tone. The room and time are illustrative details that would need to be verified in an actual announcement.
questions.rationale: Assesses audience awareness and purposeful selection of accessible language and relevant information.

questions.prompt: Choose a school or community topic that requires communication with two different audiences. Research each audience's likely needs and existing knowledge. Create two texts of 250–350 words each, or equivalent multimodal products, addressing the same core subject from a consistent, clearly established perspective. Adapt the information, organization, diction, syntax, and design for each audience. Write a 300-word commentary comparing the choices and evaluating how effectively each product fulfills its purpose.
questions.answer: Evaluate the clarity of audience and purpose, consistency and appropriateness of perspective, relevance of selected information, accessibility of design, effectiveness of diction and syntax, and the quality of the student's explanation and evaluation.
questions.rationale: Integrates interpretation and construction across the three expectations through authentic audience-based composition and rhetorical analysis.

evidence: An annotated rhetorical analysis identifying author, audience, context, purpose, and perspective.
A comparative analysis of two texts addressing the same subject for different audiences.
An audience profile documenting relevant knowledge, needs, and expectations.
A writing plan establishing purpose, perspective, and intended outcome.
Two versions of a communication adapted for different audiences.
A text-design audit evaluating accessibility and usability.
A revision commentary explaining changes to content, diction, syntax, or craft.
A reflection evaluating whether a completed text accomplishes its intended purpose.
instruction: Begin with authentic texts whose intended audiences and purposes can be reasonably established.
Teach students to support claims about audience and purpose with evidence rather than relying on unsupported guesses.
Model how an author's perspective influences which information is highlighted and how it is presented.
Use paired texts addressing similar subjects for different audiences to make rhetorical decisions visible.
Distinguish an author's intended purpose from a text's possible unintended effects.
Demonstrate how audience knowledge influences the amount of background information and explanation required.
Analyze text design alongside language, including headings, organization, navigation, typography, and meaningful visual elements.
Teach accessible communication practices, including descriptive headings, clear link labels, readable structure, and alternatives for important visual information.
Use revision exercises that require students to adapt an existing text for a new audience.
Encourage students to articulate a clear perspective without treating perspective as permission to ignore evidence.
Provide authentic school, civic, academic, and professional communication tasks.
Use peer feedback from readers who represent the intended audience whenever practical.
Ask students to explain why particular rhetorical and design choices are appropriate rather than simply naming techniques.
Assess the effectiveness of choices in relation to purpose and audience rather than rewarding complexity for its own sake.
watchFor: Treating audience identification as a guess based only on the subject of a text.
Confusing an author's purpose with the topic or genre.
Assuming every text has exactly one purpose or audience.
Treating the author's stated intention as proof that the text achieves its purpose.
Confusing a unique perspective with an unsupported opinion.
Assuming that all members of an intended audience have identical knowledge, experiences, or needs.
Reducing audience adaptation to changing a few vocabulary words.
Ignoring how information selection and omission influence a text's perspective.
Treating visually attractive design as automatically accessible or effective.
Using technical vocabulary without considering whether the audience understands it.
Overloading a text with background information irrelevant to its purpose.
Making audience-based revisions that accidentally distort evidence or change the underlying facts.
Claiming certainty about audience responses without evidence.
Evaluating a text only by whether the evaluator personally agrees with its message.
Teaching rhetorical techniques in isolation from the audience and purpose they are meant to serve.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level scores. The surviving versions of Sojourner Truth's 1851 speech differ substantially; use a reputable historical archive and teach the provenance of the versions rather than presenting one transcription as a verified verbatim record. For authentic communication tasks, evaluate usability and accessibility alongside rhetorical effectiveness.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can study how authors make their writing effective. I can identify and evaluate choices in language, sentences, structure, and design, explain their effects on readers, and use those techniques intentionally in my own writing.
know: Reading like a writer means examining how a text is constructed, not only what it communicates.
Authors make choices about literary, expository, and rhetorical elements to achieve particular effects.
Literary elements include characterization, setting, conflict, imagery, dialogue, and point of view.
Expository elements include definitions, examples, comparisons, explanations, and supporting details.
Rhetorical elements include claims, evidence, appeals, concessions, and techniques used to engage or influence audiences.
Diction influences meaning, tone, voice, and audience response.
Syntax includes the arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses within sentences.
Sentence length, variety, repetition, and punctuation can influence rhythm, emphasis, and pacing.
Text organization includes the sequence and relationship of ideas or events.
Text design includes features such as headings, paragraphing, spacing, typography, visuals, and navigation.
Accessibility concerns whether an intended audience can perceive, navigate, understand, and use a text.
A craft technique is effective when it contributes meaningfully to a text's purpose and audience.
Writers can study mentor texts, experiment with techniques, and evaluate the results in their own compositions.
understand: Authors construct experiences for readers through deliberate choices.
A reader's emotional or intellectual response can provide a starting point for investigating an author's craft.
Identifying a technique is different from analyzing how it works.
The effectiveness of a technique depends on context, audience, and purpose.
Small changes in diction or syntax can significantly change a passage's effect.
Organization and design influence both meaning and accessibility.
Reading and writing reinforce each other when students investigate techniques and apply what they discover.
Imitating a technique involves understanding its function rather than merely copying its appearance.
Effective writers evaluate whether their craft decisions produce the intended response.
do: Identify literary, expository, and rhetorical elements and analyze their effects on audiences and purposes (9.P.AC.1.a).
Apply selected literary, expository, or rhetorical techniques in original compositions (9.P.AC.1.a).
Identify significant word choices and explain how they influence meaning, tone, and audience response (9.P.AC.1.b).
Experiment with diction to produce particular effects in original writing (9.P.AC.1.b).
Analyze how sentence structure and syntax contribute to emphasis, pacing, clarity, and purpose (9.P.AC.1.c).
Apply purposeful sentence structures in original compositions and evaluate their effects (9.P.AC.1.c).
Analyze how formats, structures, patterns, and design features influence interpretation and accessibility (9.P.AC.1.d).
Make intentional organizational and design decisions when constructing texts (9.P.AC.1.d).
Support craft analysis with specific textual evidence and explanations of effects (9.P.AC.1.a–d).
Reflect on how mentor-text techniques can inform revision and independent writing (9.P.AC.1.a–d).
targets: I can identify an interesting or effective craft choice in a text.
I can explain what the author does, how it works, and why it matters.
I can analyze how literary, expository, or rhetorical elements affect readers.
I can explain the effect of particular words and phrases.
I can analyze how sentence structure influences pacing, emphasis, or tone.
I can evaluate how organization and design support a text's purpose.

vocabulary.definition: The techniques and decisions an author uses to create meaning and achieve effects.
vocabulary.example: A novelist delays revealing important information to build suspense.

vocabulary.definition: A text studied as a model for particular writing techniques.
vocabulary.example: Students study the opening of a short story before experimenting with their own openings.

vocabulary.definition: A component of literary writing that contributes to meaning or effect.
vocabulary.example: Dialogue reveals a character's personality without direct explanation.

vocabulary.definition: A method of explaining or developing information.
vocabulary.example: A science writer uses an analogy to explain an unfamiliar process.

vocabulary.definition: A communicative strategy used to achieve a purpose with an audience.
vocabulary.example: A speaker repeats a central phrase to reinforce an argument.

vocabulary.definition: The purposeful selection and use of words.
vocabulary.example: A narrator's informal vocabulary creates a conversational voice.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses within sentences.
vocabulary.example: A writer places a short sentence after several long ones to create emphasis.

vocabulary.definition: The rate at which information or events unfold in a text.

vocabulary.definition: The repetition of similar grammatical forms to express related ideas.

vocabulary.definition: The placement of contrasting elements near one another to highlight differences or relationships.

vocabulary.definition: The organization and relationship of a text's parts.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of visual elements to communicate relative importance and guide attention.
vocabulary.example: A guide uses clear headings and consistent subheadings to help readers locate information.

vocabulary.definition: The extent to which people can perceive, navigate, understand, and use a text.
vocabulary.example: Descriptive headings and meaningful link text make a digital guide easier to navigate.

vocabulary.definition: An explanation of how a specific authorial choice creates meaning or affects an audience.
