differentiation.title: Notice, name, explain
differentiation.activity: Students read a short, high-interest passage and identify three noticeable craft choices, such as repetition, a vivid verb, or a short sentence. For each choice, they complete a three-part response: what the author did, what they noticed as readers, and how the choice may have created that effect. Students then imitate one technique in two or three original sentences.
differentiation.scaffolds: Teacher think-aloud, color-coded passage, limited technique menu, sentence frames, paired discussion.
differentiation.success: Identify three craft choices, explain the likely effect of two, and use one intentionally in original writing.
differentiation.materials: Short literary passage; annotation guide; craft response organizer.

differentiation.title: The craft experiment
differentiation.activity: Students examine an excerpt from 'The Tell-Tale Heart' or another approved mentor text. They analyze diction, syntax, and narrative technique, then rewrite the excerpt using more neutral language and conventional sentence structures. After comparing versions, students write an analytical paragraph explaining how the original craft choices influence readers.
differentiation.scaffolds: Mentor-text annotations, before-and-after organizer, analytical paragraph model, peer feedback.
differentiation.success: Explain three distinct craft effects using specific textual evidence and demonstrate purposeful changes in a rewritten passage.
differentiation.materials: Mentor-text excerpt; writing document; comparison organizer.

differentiation.title: Build a writer's craft portfolio
differentiation.activity: Students select three mentor texts representing different forms, such as fiction, rhetorical nonfiction, and digital informational writing. They analyze one significant technique from each, then construct an original text incorporating at least three purposeful craft choices. Students submit annotated mentor passages, drafts, revisions, and a commentary evaluating the effectiveness of their decisions for a defined audience.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional craft-analysis framework, mentor-text selection guide, individual conferences, peer critique.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate accurate craft analysis, thoughtful adaptation of techniques, purposeful revision, and evidence-based evaluation of the final text.
differentiation.materials: Mentor texts; annotation tools; writing portfolio; reflection rubric.

questions.prompt: A suspense writer follows a long descriptive paragraph with the sentence 'The door opened.' What is the most plausible effect of this change in syntax?
options: It necessarily makes the narrator unreliable.
It can create a sudden moment of emphasis and interrupt the previous rhythm.
It removes the need for descriptive details.
It guarantees that readers will understand the ending.
questions.answer: It can create a sudden moment of emphasis and interrupt the previous rhythm.
questions.rationale: A short sentence can stand out against longer surrounding sentences, changing rhythm and directing attention.

questions.prompt: Which response best demonstrates reading like a writer?
options: The story is about a person who becomes frightened.
The story was interesting and easy to understand.
The author repeats the same phrase as the character becomes increasingly anxious, creating a sense of mounting pressure.
The main character makes an important decision near the end.
questions.answer: The author repeats the same phrase as the character becomes increasingly anxious, creating a sense of mounting pressure.
questions.rationale: The response identifies a specific craft technique and explains its contribution to the reader's experience.

questions.prompt: A digital guide has attractive illustrations but uses vague headings, unlabeled links, and long unbroken paragraphs. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The illustrations guarantee that the guide is accessible.
The guide's visual appeal eliminates the need for organization.
The design may hinder navigation and understanding despite its attractive appearance.
Text design has no relationship to the author's purpose.
questions.answer: The design may hinder navigation and understanding despite its attractive appearance.
questions.rationale: Effective design considers usability, accessibility, audience needs, and purpose, not visual attractiveness alone.

questions.prompt: Read this original passage: 'The hallway stretched ahead. Silent. Empty. Then came the footsteps.' Explain how the sentence structure and diction contribute to the passage's effect. Suggest one revision that would change the pacing.
questions.answer: A strong response explains that fragments and short sentences isolate details and may create suspense. Words such as 'silent' and 'empty' emphasize absence. A valid revision might combine sentences into a longer descriptive sentence to create a smoother, slower rhythm, with an explanation of the changed effect.
questions.rationale: Assesses analysis of diction and syntax together with the ability to make purposeful revisions.

questions.prompt: Select a 200–350-word literary, expository, or rhetorical mentor passage. Identify and analyze four craft choices: one literary, expository, or rhetorical element; one example of diction; one syntactic decision; and one organizational or design feature. Explain how each affects the intended audience and supports the text's purpose. Then construct a 350–500-word original text, or equivalent multimodal product, applying at least three of the techniques for a clearly defined audience. Submit a 250-word commentary explaining your choices and evaluating their effectiveness.
questions.answer: Evaluate accuracy and specificity of craft analysis, attention to audience and purpose, appropriate use of textual evidence, purposeful application of techniques, consideration of organization and accessibility, and quality of reflection.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through analysis, application, evaluation, and reflection.

evidence: An annotated mentor text identifying literary, expository, or rhetorical techniques and their effects.
A craft-analysis paragraph connecting a specific authorial choice to audience and purpose.
A diction experiment comparing original and revised word choices.
A syntax comparison explaining differences in rhythm, emphasis, or pacing.
An organizational or design audit addressing usability and accessibility.
An original composition incorporating techniques studied in mentor texts.
A before-and-after revision demonstrating intentional craft decisions.
A writer's commentary explaining and evaluating the effectiveness of those decisions.
instruction: Begin craft study with an authentic reader response: surprise, confusion, tension, curiosity, admiration, or another noticeable effect.
Ask students to investigate which specific authorial decisions may have produced that response.
Model the difference between identifying a technique and analyzing its function.
Use the recurring questions: What did the author do? How does it work? Why might it matter for this audience and purpose?
Select short mentor passages with craft choices students can clearly observe and experiment with.
Teach literary, expository, and rhetorical techniques across genres rather than limiting craft study to fiction.
Include diction and syntax in close-reading lessons, not only in grammar instruction.
Use imitation exercises that preserve the function of a technique while allowing students to create original content.
Compare original and revised passages to make the effects of craft choices visible.
Study organization and design in both print and digital texts.
Include accessibility considerations when evaluating digital and multimodal compositions.
Ask students to explain why a technique works in its particular context rather than labeling it universally effective.
Provide opportunities to revise original writing based on craft analysis and audience feedback.
Assess the quality of explanation and application rather than the number of literary terms students can identify.
watchFor: Reducing reading like a writer to highlighting literary devices.
Assuming that naming a technique constitutes analysis.
Treating every use of a technique as equally effective.
Claiming certainty about an author's intention without supporting evidence.
Ignoring the relationship between craft, audience, and purpose.
Discussing diction without examining the significance of particular words.
Treating syntax only as grammatical correctness rather than a resource for meaning and effect.
Assuming short sentences always create suspense or long sentences always slow pacing.
Confusing a reader's personal reaction with an effect that every reader must experience.
Using imitation exercises that reproduce copyrighted passages rather than developing original writing.
Evaluating digital design solely by its appearance.
Overlooking how headings, spacing, structure, and navigation affect accessibility.
Requiring students to use sophisticated techniques when simpler choices better serve their purpose.
Separating craft analysis from opportunities to write and revise.
Rewarding terminology more than precise observation and evidence-based explanation.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Craft analysis should examine techniques in context and distinguish observable effects from speculative claims about authorial intention. For imitation exercises, students should create original language and content while adapting the underlying technique.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can imagine how my audience will experience my writing. I can choose techniques, words, sentences, and structures that help readers understand, feel, question, or act in ways that support my purpose.
know: Writing like a reader involves anticipating how an audience may interpret and respond to a text.
Authors make craft decisions based on audience, context, and purpose.
Literary techniques can develop characters, create atmosphere, build suspense, and communicate experiences.
Expository techniques can clarify unfamiliar information through definitions, examples, comparisons, and explanations.
Rhetorical techniques can influence audiences through reasoning, evidence, appeals, and purposeful emphasis.
Word choice influences tone, meaning, emotional associations, and audience expectations.
Sentence structure and syntax influence clarity, rhythm, pacing, emphasis, and accessibility.
Text organization determines when and how audiences encounter information.
Formats and design features can help readers navigate and understand complex material.
Audience members may have different experiences, prior knowledge, reading needs, and expectations.
Writers can use feedback and reader testing to investigate how their choices are received.
A writer's intended effect may differ from an audience's actual response.
Revision involves evaluating the reader's experience and adjusting craft choices accordingly.
understand: Effective writing considers both what the writer intends and what the audience needs.
Authors influence readers through combinations of literary, expository, and rhetorical techniques.
A word or phrase can shape a reader's response without explicitly telling the reader what to think.
Sentence-level choices influence the experience of reading as well as grammatical meaning.
Organization and design can make information more accessible or create unnecessary obstacles.
A technique that works for one audience or purpose may not work for another.
Audience awareness requires informed consideration rather than assumptions about an entire group.
Feedback provides evidence about possible reader responses but does not automatically determine every revision.
Writers become more effective when they can explain the relationship between a craft choice and its intended effect.
do: Select and integrate literary, expository, and rhetorical elements appropriate to a target audience and purpose (9.P.AC.2.a).
Evaluate how combinations of craft techniques may influence an audience's experience (9.P.AC.2.a).
Choose words and phrases intended to shape audience understanding, responses, decisions, or questions (9.P.AC.2.b).
Revise diction to improve precision, tone, engagement, or persuasive effect (9.P.AC.2.b).
Construct and reshape sentences to accommodate audience needs and achieve intended effects (9.P.AC.2.c).
Evaluate the impact of sentence length, variety, arrangement, and emphasis on readability and meaning (9.P.AC.2.c).
Select organizational structures and formats appropriate to the intended audience and purpose (9.P.AC.2.d).
Use headings, transitions, paragraphing, visual features, or other relevant design elements to support accessibility (9.P.AC.2.d).
Anticipate audience questions and provide information or clarification where needed (9.P.AC.2.a–d).
Use feedback and reflection to evaluate whether writing choices support the intended reader experience (9.P.AC.2.a–d).
targets: I can identify the audience and purpose of a text I plan to create.
I can explain how I want my audience to respond to my writing.
I can select literary, expository, or rhetorical techniques that support that response.
I can choose words that create the tone and meaning I intend.
I can vary sentence structure to improve clarity, pacing, or emphasis.
I can organize information in an order that helps my audience follow my ideas.
I can use text features that make my writing accessible and easy to navigate.
I can anticipate and address likely reader questions.
I can use reader feedback to identify where my writing succeeds or needs revision.
I can justify my craft choices by connecting them to audience and purpose.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of considering readers' knowledge, needs, expectations, and possible responses when composing.
vocabulary.example: A writer explains unfamiliar terminology before presenting a technical argument.

vocabulary.definition: The process through which an audience encounters, understands, and responds to a text.
vocabulary.example: A mystery writer considers what readers know at each stage of the plot.

vocabulary.definition: An intentional choice about content, language, structure, technique, or design.
vocabulary.example: An author opens with a question to invite readers into an investigation.

vocabulary.definition: A method used to develop meaning or effect in literary writing.
vocabulary.example: A writer uses sensory imagery to establish a vivid setting.

vocabulary.definition: A method used to clarify, explain, or develop information.
vocabulary.example: A writer uses a familiar analogy to explain an unfamiliar concept.

vocabulary.definition: A communicative strategy intended to influence understanding, judgment, or action.
vocabulary.example: A speaker acknowledges a reasonable objection before responding with evidence.

vocabulary.definition: The purposeful selection of words and phrases.
vocabulary.example: A writer selects 'persistent' rather than 'stubborn' to communicate admiration.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses within sentences.
vocabulary.example: A writer places the most consequential idea at the end of a sentence for emphasis.

vocabulary.definition: The rate at which information, ideas, or events unfold for an audience.
vocabulary.example: Short sentences accelerate a tense scene, while reflection slows the narrative.

vocabulary.definition: The process of predicting what readers may expect, question, or need.
vocabulary.example: A guide answers a likely question before readers reach a complicated step.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement and relationships of a text's parts.
vocabulary.example: A proposal moves from the problem to evidence, alternatives, and a recommendation.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which people can perceive, navigate, understand, and use a text.
vocabulary.example: A digital article uses meaningful headings, descriptive links, and accessible alternatives to images.

vocabulary.definition: Information from an audience about how a text is understood or experienced.
vocabulary.example: A peer explains where an instruction was unclear or where an argument raised an unanswered question.

vocabulary.definition: An explanation of why a writer changed a text and what the change is intended to accomplish.
vocabulary.example: A student explains that moving a definition earlier helps readers understand the following argument.

differentiation.title: What will my reader need?
differentiation.activity: Students receive a short, deliberately unclear set of instructions for a familiar classroom task. They identify three likely reader questions, revise confusing words and sentences, and reorganize the instructions into clearly labeled steps. Partners test whether the revised directions are understandable.
differentiation.scaffolds: Audience question cards, teacher think-aloud, sentence-combining and splitting models, numbered-step template.
differentiation.success: Identify three reader needs and make at least three purposeful changes to wording, syntax, or organization.
differentiation.materials: Teacher-created instructions; audience checklist; revision organizer.

differentiation.title: Write for a reaction
differentiation.activity: Students select one intended audience response, such as curiosity, concern, suspense, confidence, or reconsideration. They examine a short mentor passage that produces a related effect, then write a 250-word original text using purposeful diction, syntax, and at least one literary, expository, or rhetorical technique. Peers describe their actual responses without first being told the writer's intention. Writers compare the feedback with their goals and revise.
differentiation.scaffolds: Mentor-text examples, reader-response planning chart, craft menu, structured feedback protocol.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate three intentional craft decisions, gather specific audience feedback, and justify at least two revisions.
differentiation.materials: Mentor passages; writing document; feedback and revision form.

differentiation.title: Engineer the reader's journey
differentiation.activity: Students design a 500–700-word feature article, persuasive essay, narrative, or equivalent multimodal publication for a defined audience. They map what readers should know, feel, question, or decide at several points in the text. They then select techniques, diction, syntax, organization, and accessible design features to support that progression. After testing a draft with representative readers, students revise and submit an annotated explanation of their decisions.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional audience journey map, mentor-text comparison, accessibility checklist, writing conference.
differentiation.success: Create a coherent audience-centered text, apply multiple effective craft choices, respond thoughtfully to feedback, and evaluate whether the intended reader experience was achieved.
differentiation.materials: Audience journey organizer; mentor texts; publishing tools; peer response protocol; rubric.

questions.prompt: A student is writing an article explaining a complicated school scheduling process to incoming ninth graders. Which decision best demonstrates writing like a reader?
options: Use technical abbreviations without explanation.
Begin with the most complicated exception to the policy.
Introduce essential terms, organize the process into steps, and answer likely questions.
Assume readers already understand how high school schedules work.
questions.answer: Introduce essential terms, organize the process into steps, and answer likely questions.
questions.rationale: The choice anticipates the audience's knowledge and needs while using language and organization to support understanding.

questions.prompt: A writer wants to create a sudden moment of alarm after several paragraphs of calm description. Which revision is most likely to support that effect?
options: Insert a brief, direct sentence revealing the danger.
Add an unrelated explanation of the setting's history.
Replace every verb with a more complicated synonym.
Repeat the same descriptive paragraph.
questions.answer: Insert a brief, direct sentence revealing the danger.
questions.rationale: A sudden change in syntax and information can interrupt the established rhythm and direct readers' attention.

questions.prompt: A student creates a digital article with strong arguments but no headings, vague links, and an important chart without an explanation. Which revision best addresses audience experience?
options: Add decorative graphics without changing the content.
Use meaningful headings and links and provide an accessible explanation of the chart.
Remove all evidence to make the article shorter.
Increase the complexity of the vocabulary.
questions.answer: Use meaningful headings and links and provide an accessible explanation of the chart.
questions.rationale: Accessible organizational and design features help readers navigate and understand the text.

questions.prompt: A writer wants readers to question whether a character can be trusted. Describe two specific craft choices the writer could make, using different techniques, and explain the intended effect of each.
questions.answer: A strong response might suggest including inconsistencies between the character's statements and actions, using carefully selected details that contradict the character's claims, or controlling when readers discover important information. Each choice should be linked to the audience's developing uncertainty.
questions.rationale: Assesses the ability to select and justify techniques based on a planned reader response.

questions.prompt: Revise this original opening for an audience of students who have never participated in a research project: 'The utilization of authoritative repositories facilitates the acquisition of substantiated informational resources.' Explain at least three choices you make to improve the reader's experience.
questions.answer: One possible revision is: 'Start your research with reliable sources, such as library databases. These can help you find information supported by evidence.' A strong explanation addresses more familiar diction, clearer syntax, and an example that helps the audience understand the process.
questions.rationale: Assesses audience-centered revision of diction, syntax, and explanation.

questions.prompt: Create a 500–700-word original text, or equivalent multimodal product, for a clearly defined audience and purpose. Before drafting, develop a reader-experience map identifying what you want the audience to understand, feel, question, or decide at the beginning, middle, and end. Apply at least one literary, expository, or rhetorical technique, three deliberate diction choices, two purposeful syntactic decisions, and an organizational or design feature supporting accessibility. Obtain feedback from at least two readers, revise the text, and submit a 250-word commentary evaluating the relationship between your intentions, readers' actual responses, and your final craft choices.
questions.answer: Evaluate the appropriateness of techniques for audience and purpose, effectiveness of language and syntax, clarity and accessibility of organization, evidence of meaningful revision, and the precision of the student's reflection. Do not require readers to report identical emotional responses.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through planning, construction, audience feedback, and evaluation.

evidence: An audience profile describing readers' likely knowledge, needs, and questions.
A reader-experience map showing intended responses across a text.
A writing plan connecting literary, expository, or rhetorical techniques to audience and purpose.
An annotated draft identifying purposeful diction and syntax choices.
An organizational plan or storyboard showing the intended sequence of information.
An accessibility checklist documenting relevant design decisions.
Reader feedback comparing intended and experienced effects.
A revised composition with a rationale explaining audience-centered changes.
A final writer's commentary evaluating the effectiveness of selected craft techniques.
instruction: Begin writing lessons by asking what the audience should understand, experience, question, or do after encountering the text.
Model how to anticipate reader knowledge without making unsupported assumptions about an entire audience.
Use mentor texts to examine how authors guide readers' attention and expectations.
Teach students to integrate literary, expository, and rhetorical elements as appropriate to the task rather than requiring all three in every composition.
Use diction exercises that compare how alternative words affect precision, tone, and connotation.
Demonstrate how sentence length, arrangement, and variety can change emphasis and pacing.
Teach organization as a sequence of reader experiences rather than simply a prescribed paragraph formula.
Include text design and accessibility when planning print, digital, and multimodal work.
Encourage students to identify likely reader questions and provide clarification at useful points.
Use blind reader-response exercises in which peers describe their reactions before learning the writer's intentions.
Help students distinguish useful reader feedback from suggestions that would undermine their purpose.
Model revision decisions that respond to audience needs while preserving accuracy and the writer's perspective.
Encourage writers to explain why they selected a technique rather than merely identifying it.
Evaluate audience-centered writing through observable craft choices, evidence of revision, and thoughtful reflection.
watchFor: Treating writing like a reader as simply correcting grammar and spelling.
Assuming a writer can control every reader's emotional response.
Confusing intended effect with evidence that the effect actually occurred.
Using audience stereotypes instead of considering specific needs and circumstances.
Choosing techniques because they sound sophisticated rather than because they serve a purpose.
Using emotionally charged language that misrepresents evidence or distorts factual claims.
Making word substitutions that unintentionally change meaning.
Assuming that short sentences always create urgency or long sentences always improve explanation.
Following a rigid organizational template when another structure would better serve readers.
Confusing attractive design with accessible design.
Overloading a text with decorative features that interfere with comprehension.
Asking for audience feedback without teaching readers to provide specific observations.
Accepting every peer suggestion without evaluating its relationship to the writer's purpose.
Revising only at the sentence level when structural changes are necessary.
Grading a writer solely on whether an audience reacts exactly as predicted.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. The purpose of mentor-text study is to understand and adapt techniques in original compositions, not to reproduce protected expression. Reader responses can vary; assess the quality of audience-centered decisions and reflection rather than requiring uniform reactions.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can explain how the format, genre, organization, and features of a text influence its meaning and audience. I can choose and combine words, images, sounds, and other elements to create texts that communicate effectively.
know: Mode refers to a means of communicating meaning, such as linguistic, visual, aural, gestural, or spatial communication.
Genre refers to a recognizable type of text associated with particular purposes, conventions, and audience expectations.
A text's mode and genre influence the information its creator includes.
A text's mode and genre influence how information is organized and presented.
Multimodal texts combine two or more modes of communication.
Text features may include headings, captions, diagrams, illustrations, hyperlinks, typography, and navigation elements.
Design choices influence meaning, tone, style, audience engagement, and purpose.
Genre conventions provide useful expectations but can be adapted or combined.
Visual hierarchy helps readers distinguish important information from supporting details.
The arrangement of information influences what audiences notice first and how they understand relationships.
Images, audio, and visual elements can contribute information not expressed in words.
Multimodal elements should complement or extend meaning rather than merely decorate a text.
Accessibility is an essential consideration in text design.
Effective text design depends on audience needs, communication goals, and the circumstances in which a text will be used.
understand: Design is part of meaning-making, not simply the decoration added after writing.
Different modes and genres offer different possibilities and limitations for communicating ideas.
Choosing a genre involves deciding what information belongs in the text and how audiences expect to encounter it.
A text's structure and features can reinforce or undermine its purpose.
Multimodal texts require coordination among their different elements.
An image, chart, or audio element should be evaluated for its contribution to meaning.
A design that is attractive to one audience may be confusing or inaccessible to another.
Writers and designers can adapt genre conventions while maintaining clarity.
Evaluating text design requires examining the relationship among content, structure, features, audience, and purpose.
do: Explore texts representing different modes and genres and identify their characteristic features (9.P.AC.3.a).
Explain how specific design features affect meaning, tone, style, purpose, and audience (9.P.AC.3.a).
Create texts that intentionally use the features of selected modes and genres (9.P.AC.3.a).
Analyze how mode and genre influence which ideas, details, and information are included or omitted (9.P.AC.3.b).
Select information appropriate to the conventions and purpose of a chosen mode and genre (9.P.AC.3.b).
Analyze how mode and genre influence the sequence, arrangement, and relationships of ideas (9.P.AC.3.c).
Organize original texts using structures and arrangements appropriate to their mode, genre, and audience (9.P.AC.3.c).
Interpret multimodal texts by explaining how their elements work together to create meaning (9.P.AC.3.d).
Construct multimodal texts integrating appropriate genres, features, and craft techniques (9.P.AC.3.d).
Evaluate and revise text designs to improve clarity, accessibility, audience engagement, and effectiveness (9.P.AC.3.a–d).
targets: I can distinguish between a text's mode and its genre.
I can identify design features and explain their effects.
I can explain why different genres include different kinds of information.
I can analyze how the arrangement of information influences understanding.
I can compare how the same subject is presented in different modes or genres.
I can choose a suitable mode and genre for a particular purpose.
I can select and organize information according to audience needs.
I can explain how words, images, sounds, or other elements work together.
I can create a purposeful multimodal text.
I can revise a design to improve accessibility and effectiveness.

vocabulary.definition: A means of communicating meaning, such as linguistic, visual, aural, gestural, or spatial expression.
vocabulary.example: A podcast relies heavily on linguistic and aural modes.

vocabulary.definition: A recognizable category of text associated with particular purposes and conventions.
vocabulary.example: A scientific report and a personal narrative use different conventions.

vocabulary.definition: A text that combines two or more modes of communication.
vocabulary.example: An educational video combines spoken explanation, written labels, and animation.

vocabulary.definition: An element that helps organize, clarify, navigate, or communicate information.
vocabulary.example: A diagram caption explains what the diagram represents.

vocabulary.definition: A characteristic pattern or expectation associated with a genre.
vocabulary.example: A news report commonly identifies essential information early.

vocabulary.definition: The arrangement of visual elements to communicate relative importance.
vocabulary.example: A prominent headline directs attention to the article's central subject.

vocabulary.definition: The spatial arrangement of text and other elements.
vocabulary.example: A comparison chart places corresponding information in adjacent columns.

vocabulary.definition: The selection and arrangement of type to support readability and visual communication.
vocabulary.example: Consistent heading styles help readers understand a document's structure.

vocabulary.definition: Text accompanying an image, chart, or other element to explain or contextualize it.
vocabulary.example: A photograph's caption identifies the event and date.

vocabulary.definition: A visual presentation combining information, data, and design elements to communicate ideas.
vocabulary.example: An infographic compares changes in library circulation over several years.

vocabulary.definition: A sequence of planned frames or sections representing the organization of a visual or multimodal text.
vocabulary.example: Students storyboard an informational video before recording it.

vocabulary.definition: The features and pathways that help users move through a text or digital resource.
vocabulary.example: A table of contents links readers to sections of a research guide.

vocabulary.definition: The extent to which a text can be perceived, navigated, understood, and used by people with different needs.
vocabulary.example: A video includes accurate captions and avoids communicating essential information through color alone.

vocabulary.definition: A capability or opportunity a mode, medium, or format offers for communication.
vocabulary.example: An interactive map allows users to explore geographic relationships that may be difficult to explain in prose alone.
