suggestedTexts.access: Licensed anthology or authorized excerpt; provide relevant historical sources and opportunities for critical evaluation.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A collection uses different forms of writing to explore historical questions
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the choice to combine essays, poetry, and other forms affect the reader's experience of the collection?

suggestedTexts.title: The Danger of a Single Story
suggestedTexts.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare how spoken delivery, timing, audience response, and written transcription shape meaning.
suggestedTexts.access: Official TED recording and authorized transcript.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: The same message can be experienced as a live performance or a written text
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What communicative information is available in the video that is less visible in the transcript?

suggestedTexts.title: National Park Service Park Maps and Visitor Guides
suggestedTexts.author: United States National Park Service
suggestedTexts.genre: Public information maps and visitor guides
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how maps, symbols, labels, warnings, and spatial arrangement help visitors make decisions.
suggestedTexts.access: Official National Park Service publications; select a current guide.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A map communicates practical information that would be cumbersome in paragraph form
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which information is communicated most effectively through spatial design, and what additional text does the audience need?

suggestedTexts.title: NASA Climate Change: Evidence
suggestedTexts.author: NASA
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate how explanatory prose, data visualizations, headings, and linked resources communicate scientific evidence.
suggestedTexts.access: Official NASA Science website; verify the current page and data.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Scientific claims are presented through a combination of explanation and visual evidence
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the visual elements extend the written explanation, and what might readers misunderstand without clear labels or context?

suggestedTexts.title: A Student-Facing Course Catalog
suggestedTexts.author: School counseling and academic departments
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate how search tools, course categories, descriptions, headings, and navigation influence students' ability to make informed choices.
suggestedTexts.access: Use a current publicly available school course catalog and verify all course information.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Students investigate whether an actual school resource helps them find the information they need
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How would you redesign this catalog for students selecting courses for the first time?

differentiation.title: Same information, different design
differentiation.activity: Students compare a short paragraph explaining a process with a labeled diagram and a numbered instruction sheet covering the same information. They identify the mode, genre, and useful features of each. They then reorganize a short paragraph into a clearly labeled sequence of steps.
differentiation.scaffolds: Teacher-created examples, visual comparison chart, limited feature vocabulary, model transformation.
differentiation.success: Identify at least three meaningful design differences and explain how two affect an audience's understanding.
differentiation.materials: Paragraph, diagram, instructions, comparison organizer.

differentiation.title: Remix the message
differentiation.activity: Students select an informational article and transform its central ideas into an infographic, a short audio script with accompanying visual plan, or a digital guide. They decide what information to preserve, condense, emphasize, or reorganize. Students then explain how the new mode and genre shaped those choices.
differentiation.scaffolds: Information-selection organizer, genre examples, design checklist, peer feedback.
differentiation.success: Preserve factual accuracy, select an appropriate structure, integrate meaningful features, and justify at least three design decisions.
differentiation.materials: Source article, storyboard or layout template, composition tools.

differentiation.title: Design a multimodal information experience
differentiation.activity: Students identify an authentic information need among high school students, such as understanding graduation requirements, locating research databases, or navigating an application process. They evaluate two existing examples, interview or survey a small number of potential users when feasible, and develop a multimodal guide combining written information with purposeful visual or audio elements. They test its usability and revise the design.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional audience-research protocol, design planning sheet, accessibility checklist, feedback conference.
differentiation.success: Produce an accurate, coherent, accessible multimodal resource whose genre, information selection, organization, and features serve a clearly defined audience and purpose.
differentiation.materials: Credible sources, design or publishing tools, usability checklist, rubric.

questions.prompt: Students need to understand how three bus routes connect across a city. Which format would most directly communicate the geographic relationships?
options: A paragraph listing unrelated facts about transportation
A labeled route map with a clear legend
A poem describing the experience of riding a bus
A photograph without labels or context
questions.answer: A labeled route map with a clear legend
questions.rationale: A spatial representation is well suited to showing route locations and connections, while labels and a legend help audiences interpret the information.

questions.prompt: A student adapts a detailed research article into an infographic. Which decision best demonstrates understanding of genre?
options: Copy every paragraph into small text boxes.
Remove source information because visuals never need evidence.
Select the most relevant findings and present them through clearly labeled visual comparisons.
Use as many decorative images as possible.
questions.answer: Select the most relevant findings and present them through clearly labeled visual comparisons.
questions.rationale: The student adjusts information selection and arrangement to suit the genre while retaining meaningful content.

questions.prompt: Which example most clearly demonstrates purposeful multimodal composition?
options: A presentation with unrelated background music and decorative animations
A video that combines accurate narration, labeled diagrams, and captions to explain a process
An essay with randomly selected photographs
A poster using multiple fonts but providing no essential information
questions.answer: A video that combines accurate narration, labeled diagrams, and captions to explain a process
questions.rationale: The different modes work together to communicate information, support understanding, and improve access.

questions.prompt: A written transcript and a video recording present the same public speech. Identify two differences in how audiences may experience the versions and explain how those differences influence meaning or interpretation.
questions.answer: A strong response might discuss vocal emphasis, pauses, gestures, facial expression, pacing, or audience reaction in the recording, compared with the transcript's opportunities for rereading, annotation, and searching. Each difference should be linked to a specific interpretive effect.
questions.rationale: Assesses analysis of how mode and features influence meaning and audience experience.

questions.prompt: Compare an informational article and an infographic addressing the same topic. Explain one important difference in information selection, one difference in organization, and one advantage or limitation of each format for its intended audience.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies concrete examples, explains how genre influences content and arrangement, and evaluates the formats in relation to purpose rather than assuming one is universally superior.
questions.rationale: Assesses understanding of genre-based information selection and organization.

questions.prompt: Choose a topic relevant to students and investigate it using at least three credible sources. Create two products communicating the same essential information in different genres or modes. At least one must be multimodal. For example, produce a 400-word explanatory article and an infographic, or a digital guide and a short captioned video. Include accurate source attribution and accessible design features. Write a 300-word design commentary comparing the information selected, organizational decisions, specific features, and intended effects of the two products.
questions.answer: Evaluate factual accuracy, genre and mode awareness, purposeful information selection, appropriate organization, effective integration of multimodal elements, accessibility, and the student's ability to explain design decisions in relation to audience and purpose.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through comparative interpretation, text construction, multimodal design, and reflection.

evidence: A comparison chart identifying the modes, genres, and characteristic features of several texts.
An annotated text explaining how design features influence meaning, tone, style, or purpose.
An analysis comparing information selection across two genres.
A structural comparison explaining how different formats organize similar information.
A storyboard or wireframe for an original multimodal text.
An original infographic, digital guide, podcast, video, or other purposeful multimodal product.
An accessibility review documenting meaningful design choices.
A revision record showing changes made after audience or usability feedback.
A design commentary explaining how mode and genre shaped content and organization.
instruction: Introduce text design by comparing two authentic texts addressing the same subject through different modes or genres.
Teach mode and genre as related but distinct concepts.
Ask students what a chosen format makes easier or harder to communicate.
Analyze information selection before examining visual appearance.
Model how genre conventions influence the sequence and arrangement of ideas.
Examine how headings, captions, charts, diagrams, audio, and navigation features contribute to meaning.
Use graphic novels, recorded speeches, informational websites, maps, and data visualizations alongside conventional prose.
Teach students to evaluate the relationship between visual evidence and accompanying explanations.
Provide opportunities to transform a text from one mode or genre into another.
Require students to preserve accuracy when condensing or adapting source material.
Use storyboards and wireframes to plan multimodal texts before production.
Teach relevant accessibility practices, including captions, meaningful headings, readable contrast, descriptive links, and alternatives to essential visual information.
Include authentic audiences and purposes whenever possible.
Use peer feedback and usability testing to identify confusion or design barriers.
Assess the effectiveness of communication rather than the sophistication of the software used.
watchFor: Confusing mode with genre.
Treating text design as decoration rather than meaning-making.
Assuming multimodal means simply adding a picture to an essay.
Assuming every digital text is automatically multimodal.
Focusing on visual attractiveness while neglecting accuracy or purpose.
Copying all information from one genre into another without considering selection and arrangement.
Using charts or images without explaining what they represent.
Allowing decorative elements to compete with essential information.
Using color as the only means of communicating a distinction.
Using vague hyperlinks or unclear navigation.
Presenting data without sources, labels, units, or necessary context.
Assuming that fewer words always improve communication.
Treating genre conventions as inflexible rules.
Evaluating multimodal projects primarily by production quality rather than communication effectiveness.
Ignoring the needs of audiences who cannot access particular visual or audio elements.
Failing to consider whether the chosen mode and genre are appropriate for the intended audience.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Include both literary and functional multimodal texts so students experience how mode and genre shape communication across contexts. When evaluating or constructing multimodal work, prioritize meaning, accuracy, accessibility, and audience needs over decorative complexity.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can prepare for discussions and group projects, work with others to set goals and expectations, contribute thoughtful ideas, listen and respond to different perspectives, and help my group investigate questions, solve problems, and create meaningful work.
know: Collaboration involves working with others toward a shared goal or product.
Preparation may include reading assigned texts, researching a question, developing ideas, and bringing relevant evidence.
Group norms establish expectations for participation, communication, respect, and accountability.
Shared goals identify what a group intends to accomplish.
Procedures help a group organize tasks, make decisions, manage time, and monitor progress.
Productive collaboration requires both contributing ideas and considering the ideas of others.
Active listening involves attending to another person's meaning and responding accurately.
Constructive feedback is specific, relevant, respectful, and directed toward improvement.
Questions can clarify ideas, deepen inquiry, reveal assumptions, and move a discussion forward.
Disagreement can strengthen collaborative thinking when participants use evidence and respectful reasoning.
Collaborative inquiry involves investigating questions through discussion, research, and shared analysis.
Shared projects require coordination and accountability, but equitable contribution does not always mean identical tasks.
Groups can collaborate to interpret texts, construct texts, evaluate information, and solve authentic problems.
Reflection helps collaborators evaluate both the quality of the work and the effectiveness of their process.
understand: Successful collaboration requires intentional preparation and participation.
Group norms and procedures can improve both productivity and the quality of discussion.
Collaboration is more than dividing work into separate pieces; it involves developing understanding together.
Listening and responding thoughtfully are intellectual contributions.
Differences in perspective can lead to stronger interpretations and solutions.
Evidence-based disagreement can advance a group's thinking without becoming personal conflict.
Clear goals and accountability help groups manage complex tasks.
Effective collaborators adjust their roles and approaches to support shared progress.
Feedback is most useful when it provides a specific basis for revision or reconsideration.
A successful group product does not necessarily demonstrate that every member participated meaningfully.
Collaborative skills can be learned, practiced, observed, and improved.
do: Prepare for discussions and meetings by completing assigned reading, gathering evidence, and developing relevant questions or ideas (9.P.CP.1.a).
Participate actively and purposefully in group discussions and collaborative meetings (9.P.CP.1.a).
Work with peers to establish and apply group norms, shared goals, and procedures (9.P.CP.1.b).
Use collaborative planning and progress monitoring to support productive shared work (9.P.CP.1.b).
Contribute ideas and relevant evidence during discussions and projects (9.P.CP.1.c).
Listen accurately to others, acknowledge contributions, and respond to their ideas (9.P.CP.1.c).
Provide and respond to specific, constructive feedback (9.P.CP.1.c).
Collaborate to explore and interpret literary, informational, and multimodal texts (9.P.CP.1.d).
Investigate questions and evaluate possible solutions through shared inquiry (9.P.CP.1.d).
Plan, draft, revise, or produce texts collaboratively while maintaining a coherent shared purpose (9.P.CP.1.d).
Reflect on individual contributions, group processes, and the quality of collaborative outcomes (9.P.CP.1.a–d).
targets: I can arrive at a discussion with relevant preparation and evidence.
I can help my group establish clear goals and workable norms.
I can participate in decisions about roles, procedures, and deadlines.
I can contribute ideas that advance the group's thinking.
I can listen carefully and accurately summarize another person's idea.
I can ask questions that clarify or deepen discussion.
I can disagree respectfully and support my reasoning with evidence.
I can give useful feedback and respond constructively to feedback I receive.
I can work with others to investigate questions and solve problems.
I can help create a coherent shared text or project.
I can evaluate my own contribution and suggest improvements to our collaboration.

vocabulary.definition: Working with others to develop understanding or accomplish a shared goal.
vocabulary.example: Students jointly investigate a literary question and construct an evidence-based interpretation.

vocabulary.definition: Shared expectations that guide participation, communication, and accountability.
vocabulary.example: Group members agree to invite contributions, cite evidence, and respond respectfully.

vocabulary.definition: An outcome that members of a group work toward together.
vocabulary.example: A group aims to produce a well-supported comparison of two poems.

vocabulary.definition: An agreed-upon process for organizing or completing collaborative work.
vocabulary.example: A group begins meetings by reviewing progress and ends by assigning next steps.

vocabulary.definition: Responsibility for fulfilling commitments and contributing to shared progress.
vocabulary.example: Each member completes an agreed research task and explains the findings to the group.

vocabulary.definition: Attentive listening that seeks to understand and respond meaningfully to another person's ideas.
vocabulary.example: A student paraphrases a peer's interpretation before offering a different reading.

vocabulary.definition: Specific observations and suggestions intended to improve thinking, communication, or work.
vocabulary.example: A peer identifies an unsupported claim and suggests where additional evidence is needed.

vocabulary.definition: A shared investigation in which participants develop questions, examine evidence, and construct understanding.
vocabulary.example: A group researches how a historical event influenced several literary works.

vocabulary.definition: A decision or position that group members can support after considering relevant ideas and concerns.
vocabulary.example: After evaluating alternatives, a group agrees on the strongest interpretation.

vocabulary.definition: A conversation in which claims and interpretations are supported by relevant information.
vocabulary.example: Students refer to specific passages when debating a character's motivation.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of helping a group communicate, remain focused, and make progress.
vocabulary.example: A facilitator invites quieter participants to contribute and redirects an off-topic conversation.

vocabulary.definition: The integration of multiple ideas or sources into a coherent understanding.
vocabulary.example: A group combines several interpretations into a nuanced explanation.

vocabulary.definition: A process in which peers examine work and provide feedback for improvement.
vocabulary.example: Students exchange draft editorials and offer evidence-based revision suggestions.

vocabulary.definition: Thoughtful evaluation of experiences, decisions, processes, or outcomes.
vocabulary.example: A student identifies which discussion strategy helped the group resolve a disagreement.

suggestedTexts.title: Twelve Angry Men
suggestedTexts.author: Reginald Rose
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how participants in a high-stakes discussion question assumptions, challenge evidence, negotiate disagreement, and influence collective reasoning.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed play or authorized excerpt.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A jury must reach a decision while confronting conflicting interpretations of evidence
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which discussion behaviors improve the group's reasoning, and which behaviors interfere with it?

suggestedTexts.title: The Crucible
suggestedTexts.author: Arthur Miller
suggestedTexts.context: American literature · 1953; set during the Salem witch trials
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze the effects of group pressure, authority, fear, and unsupported accusations on collective decision-making.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed play or authorized excerpt.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A community's escalating accusations reveal the dangers of conformity and fear
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the characters' discussion practices prevent careful investigation and responsible decisions?

suggestedTexts.title: The Outsiders
suggestedTexts.author: S. E. Hinton
suggestedTexts.purpose: Explore how shared identities, group expectations, loyalty, and conflicting perspectives affect relationships and decisions.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed novel or authorized excerpt.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Teenagers navigate friendship, loyalty, conflict, and social divisions
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: When does group loyalty support individuals, and when does it prevent them from considering alternative perspectives?

suggestedTexts.title: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
suggestedTexts.author: William Kamkwamba and Bryan Mealer
suggestedTexts.purpose: Investigate the relationship among independent inquiry, shared knowledge, practical support, and problem-solving.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed book or authorized excerpt; a young readers edition is available.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A teenager combines reading, experimentation, and help from others to address a practical challenge
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do different forms of knowledge and contribution support the development of a solution?

suggestedTexts.title: The Danger of a Single Story
suggestedTexts.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
suggestedTexts.purpose: Support collaborative discussion about incomplete narratives, assumptions, and the value of multiple perspectives.
suggestedTexts.access: Official TED talk and authorized transcript.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A speaker challenges the limitations of familiar narratives about people and places
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How can discussion partners help one another recognize assumptions that an individual reader might overlook?

suggestedTexts.title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
suggestedTexts.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
suggestedTexts.purpose: Provide an ethically complex text for evidence-based dialogue in which multiple interpretations can be considered.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed anthology or authorized text.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A prosperous society depends on a troubling arrangement
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How can a group explore competing ethical interpretations without requiring every member to agree?

suggestedTexts.title: A Collaborative Investigative News Project
suggestedTexts.author: Student journalists or professional investigative reporting teams
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how research, fact-checking, editing, interviews, and shared planning contribute to a coherent published product.
suggestedTexts.access: Select a credible published investigation with documented reporting methods and appropriate content.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A complex story becomes possible because multiple people contribute different expertise
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which parts of this reporting process require collaboration rather than simply dividing the writing among individuals?

suggestedTexts.title: A Student Literary Magazine
suggestedTexts.author: Student writers and editors
suggestedTexts.purpose: Explore how editorial boards establish criteria, offer feedback, select submissions, and produce a coherent shared publication.
suggestedTexts.access: Use an authorized student publication with appropriate permissions.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Students make real editorial decisions about which writing to publish and how to present it
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How can an editorial team maintain shared standards while respecting different creative voices?

differentiation.title: Prepared, heard, and included
differentiation.activity: Students read a short passage independently and record one interpretation, one piece of evidence, and one question. In groups of three, they establish two discussion norms and use a structured round-robin to share ideas. Each student must accurately paraphrase a peer's contribution before adding a new idea. The group creates a two-sentence interpretation reflecting its discussion.
differentiation.scaffolds: Short accessible passage, preparation organizer, discussion stems, assigned turn-taking, teacher modeling.
differentiation.success: Arrive with prepared evidence, contribute an idea, accurately acknowledge another contribution, and help produce a shared interpretation.
differentiation.materials: Short text; discussion organizer; group norms card; shared response sheet.

differentiation.title: Literary inquiry team
differentiation.activity: Groups of four investigate a debatable interpretive question about a shared literary text. Students prepare individual claims and evidence before meeting. Each group establishes norms, assigns flexible responsibilities, examines competing interpretations, and produces a collaborative analytical paragraph or discussion brief. Students provide peer feedback and complete an individual reflection.
differentiation.scaffolds: Inquiry question bank, evidence organizer, discussion protocol, collaborative writing template, peer feedback guide.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate preparation, meaningful contribution, evidence-based dialogue, constructive feedback, and a coherent group product.
differentiation.materials: Shared literary text; discussion organizer; collaborative writing document; reflection form.

differentiation.title: Student editorial collective
differentiation.activity: Students form an editorial team to create a themed literary or cultural publication. They establish an editorial mission, selection criteria, group norms, deadlines, and a decision-making process. Members solicit or create original pieces, evaluate submissions, provide revision feedback, fact-check relevant claims, and collaboratively design a publication. Each student maintains a contribution log and submits an individual reflection on the group's decisions and process.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional editorial charter, project timeline, submission rubric, publication template, teacher conferences.
differentiation.success: Produce a coherent publication through documented collaborative inquiry, responsible decision-making, constructive feedback, and equitable participation.
differentiation.materials: Editorial planning documents; submission and feedback forms; shared publishing tools; contribution logs.

questions.prompt: A group will discuss whether a character's final decision was justified. Which student is best prepared to participate?
options: A student who plans to read the story after the discussion
A student who brings a claim, relevant textual evidence, and a question about an alternative interpretation
A student who has already decided that no other interpretation is acceptable
A student who intends to let classmates complete the discussion
questions.answer: A student who brings a claim, relevant textual evidence, and a question about an alternative interpretation
questions.rationale: Preparation includes developing ideas, gathering relevant evidence, and considering questions that support active discussion.

questions.prompt: A group project is falling behind because members disagree about responsibilities. What is the most productive next step?
options: Allow the loudest member to make every decision.
Stop discussing the project until the deadline.
Revisit the shared goal, clarify responsibilities, and agree on a workable procedure for monitoring progress.
Assign all remaining work to the fastest writer.
questions.answer: Revisit the shared goal, clarify responsibilities, and agree on a workable procedure for monitoring progress.
questions.rationale: Effective collaboration requires shared goals, agreed procedures, and attention to productivity.

questions.prompt: During a discussion, a classmate presents an interpretation you disagree with. Which response best supports collaborative inquiry?
options: That interpretation is obviously wrong.
I hear your point about the character's fear. How do you interpret the passage where the character chooses to return?
We should stop discussing this because we disagree.
My interpretation is correct because I spoke first.
questions.answer: I hear your point about the character's fear. How do you interpret the passage where the character chooses to return?
questions.rationale: The response acknowledges the other person's idea, introduces textual evidence, and invites further reasoning.

questions.prompt: A group of four students produces a strong presentation, but one member completed almost all the research and writing. Explain why the final product alone is insufficient evidence of effective collaboration. Recommend two changes to the group's process.
questions.answer: A strong response recognizes that the quality of a product does not establish whether members prepared, participated, or shared responsibility. Improvements might include agreed roles, progress checkpoints, individual preparation records, rotating responsibilities, or structured opportunities for each member to contribute.
questions.rationale: Assesses understanding of collaborative norms, accountability, and shared procedures.

questions.prompt: Read a short scene from a play in which several characters must make a collective decision. Identify one behavior that improves the group's reasoning and one that undermines it. Explain each effect using evidence from the scene, then propose a discussion norm that would improve the group's process.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies specific behaviors such as questioning evidence, acknowledging concerns, interrupting, relying on assumptions, or pressuring others. It explains the consequences of those behaviors and proposes a relevant, actionable norm.
questions.rationale: Connects interpretation of a text with analysis of collaborative practices.

questions.prompt: In a group of three or four, investigate a debatable literary, cultural, or school-related question. Before meeting, each student must prepare at least two relevant sources or passages, an initial interpretation, and two inquiry questions. Establish written group norms, a shared goal, responsibilities, and a timeline. Conduct and document at least two collaborative discussions, consider competing interpretations or solutions, provide feedback, and produce a coherent 600–800-word analytical report or equivalent multimodal product. Each member must submit an individual preparation record, contribution log, and 250-word reflection evaluating the group's process and personal contributions.
questions.answer: Evaluate individual preparation, the quality of group norms and procedures, meaningful participation, active listening, evidence-based exchange, constructive feedback, shared inquiry, the coherence of the final product, and thoughtful individual reflection. Use individual evidence of contribution alongside the group product.
questions.rationale: Integrates all four expectations through authentic collaborative inquiry, shared production, and individual accountability.

evidence: An individual discussion preparation sheet containing claims, evidence, and questions.
A collaboratively developed group charter establishing norms, goals, and procedures.
A project plan documenting responsibilities, milestones, and progress.
Teacher observation notes or a discussion transcript showing contributions and responses to peers.
An evidence-based group interpretation or inquiry summary.
Peer feedback demonstrating specific, constructive responses to others' work.
A collaboratively created literary, informational, or multimodal text.
Individual contribution records documenting preparation and participation.
A reflection identifying effective group practices and needed improvements.
instruction: Teach collaboration explicitly rather than assuming students already know how to work productively in groups.
Distinguish collaboration from dividing a project into unrelated individual tasks.
Require manageable individual preparation before collaborative discussions.
Model how to establish clear group norms, goals, procedures, and responsibilities.
Use authentic interpretive questions that benefit from considering multiple perspectives.
Teach active listening through paraphrasing, clarifying questions, and accurate acknowledgment of others' ideas.
Provide sentence stems for respectful disagreement and evidence-based response.
Use structured discussion protocols initially, then gradually increase student responsibility for managing the process.
Rotate facilitation and other responsibilities so students practice different collaborative skills.
Teach students to provide feedback that identifies a specific strength, concern, or possible improvement.
Allow students to revise interpretations when peers present persuasive evidence.
Build checkpoints into extended projects to address problems before deadlines.
Provide multiple participation pathways, including written preparation, small-group dialogue, and shared drafting.
Use individual reflection and contribution evidence to distinguish personal learning from group performance.
Evaluate both the collaborative process and the quality of the resulting inquiry or text.
watchFor: Assuming that placing students in groups automatically creates collaboration.
Equating frequent speaking with meaningful contribution.
Allowing confident speakers to dominate while others have limited opportunities to participate.
Requiring students to agree rather than teaching them to explore evidence-based disagreement.
Treating respectful disagreement as interpersonal conflict.
Using group roles that permanently assign intellectual work to some students and clerical work to others.
Confusing equal participation with identical tasks or identical speaking time.
Grading all members solely on the quality of a shared product.
Failing to establish expectations for preparation and accountability.
Using vague feedback such as 'good job' without specific observations.
Allowing group discussions to drift without a clear inquiry question or goal.
Mistaking a quick consensus for a well-supported conclusion.
Requiring students to disclose personal experiences when a text-based or hypothetical example would serve the same purpose.
Overstructuring discussions so students never learn to manage collaboration independently.
Ignoring accessibility, language needs, or other barriers to participation.
Treating a quiet but prepared and thoughtful participant as automatically disengaged.
Failing to address unequal workloads until the project is complete.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, and age suitability. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Texts about group decision-making can provide valuable models and counterexamples, but the primary evidence for this standard should come from students' actual collaborative preparation, discussions, feedback, inquiry, and shared work. Assess individual participation and growth alongside the quality of group products.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can present ideas and texts clearly for different audiences. I can choose effective ways to communicate, adjust my voice and delivery, respond thoughtfully to questions, and recite meaningful poetry and speeches with understanding.
know: A presentation communicates ideas, information, or texts to an audience for a particular purpose.
Effective presenters consider the audience's prior knowledge, interests, expectations, and needs.
A clear presentation has a focused purpose and an organization that helps listeners follow ideas.
Speakers use relevant evidence, examples, and explanations to support understanding.
Presentations may combine spoken language, written text, images, audio, demonstrations, and other modes.
Genre influences the conventions and expectations of a presentation.
Tone communicates a speaker's attitude toward the subject and audience.
Pace is the speed at which speech is delivered and can be varied for clarity and effect.
Pauses, emphasis, volume, and articulation can help audiences interpret meaning.
Nonverbal communication may include gestures, posture, facial expression, and purposeful movement.
Delivery choices should support communication rather than distract from it.
Audience questions can reveal uncertainty, disagreement, curiosity, or a need for further explanation.
Effective presenters listen to questions and respond accurately, respectfully, and with relevant evidence.
Reciting significant poetry and speeches can deepen knowledge of language, rhythm, rhetoric, and historical or literary context.
Preparation, rehearsal, feedback, and reflection support improvement in presentation skills.
understand: Effective presentation depends on the relationship among speaker, audience, purpose, and context.
Clear communication requires deliberate choices about information, organization, language, and delivery.
Different purposes may call for different presentation modes and genres.
Tone, pace, and nonverbal communication influence how audiences interpret spoken messages.
Strong delivery supports ideas rather than replacing accurate content or thoughtful reasoning.
Presentation is interactive when speakers attend to audience responses and questions.
A speaker can acknowledge uncertainty without losing credibility.
Recitation is an opportunity to interpret and understand significant texts, not merely repeat memorized words.
Presenters can develop effective individual styles without imitating one narrow model of public speaking.
Accessibility and audience needs should shape presentation planning and delivery.
do: Present ideas, information, and texts clearly and coherently for a defined audience and purpose (9.P.CP.2.a).
Organize spoken content and select appropriate supporting details to improve audience understanding (9.P.CP.2.a).
Select and integrate presentation modes and genres suited to a communication task (9.P.CP.2.b).
Use relevant visual, written, audio, or other supporting elements to extend meaning rather than merely decorate a presentation (9.P.CP.2.b).
Adjust tone, pace, emphasis, and appropriate nonverbal communication to serve purpose and audience (9.P.CP.2.c).
Rehearse and evaluate delivery choices for clarity, engagement, and effectiveness (9.P.CP.2.c).
Invite, interpret, and answer audience questions with relevant information and respectful reasoning (9.P.CP.2.d).
Ask appropriate questions to clarify audience perspectives or advance dialogue (9.P.CP.2.d).
Study the context, meaning, structure, and language of significant poems or speeches before reciting them (9.P.CP.2.e).
Recite all or part of a significant poem or speech using delivery choices informed by understanding of the text (9.P.CP.2.e).
Use feedback and self-reflection to improve presentation content, format, and delivery (9.P.CP.2.a–e).
targets: I can explain my presentation's purpose and identify its intended audience.
I can organize ideas so listeners can follow my reasoning.
I can present information clearly using relevant details and evidence.
I can choose an appropriate format and combine communication modes purposefully.
I can adjust tone and pace to support meaning.
I can use nonverbal communication appropriately without distracting from my message.
I can listen to audience questions and respond thoughtfully.
I can ask questions that support productive audience dialogue.
I can explain the meaning and context of a significant poem or speech.
I can recite a meaningful passage with interpretation and purposeful delivery.
I can evaluate my presentation and identify specific improvements.

vocabulary.definition: A planned communication of ideas, information, or texts to an audience.
vocabulary.example: A student explains the findings of a literary research project.

vocabulary.definition: The people who receive or participate in a communication.
vocabulary.example: A student adjusts explanations when presenting to incoming ninth graders.

vocabulary.definition: The outcome or effect a communicator intends to accomplish.
vocabulary.example: A presentation seeks to help classmates evaluate competing interpretations of a novel.

vocabulary.definition: A means of communicating meaning, such as linguistic, visual, aural, gestural, or spatial expression.
vocabulary.example: A presentation combines spoken explanation with a labeled diagram.

vocabulary.definition: A recognizable type of communication associated with particular conventions.
vocabulary.example: A literary reading, scientific briefing, and persuasive speech have different expectations.

vocabulary.definition: The attitude communicated through language or delivery.
vocabulary.example: A speaker adopts a measured, serious tone when discussing a sensitive issue.

vocabulary.definition: The rate at which speech is delivered.
vocabulary.example: A presenter slows down while explaining a complex process.

vocabulary.definition: Special attention given to words, phrases, or ideas through delivery.
vocabulary.example: A speaker stresses a key contrast in a sentence.

vocabulary.definition: The clear formation of speech sounds.
vocabulary.example: A presenter practices unfamiliar terminology before a research presentation.

vocabulary.definition: Meaning conveyed through gestures, posture, facial expression, movement, or other nonspoken behavior.
vocabulary.example: A speaker gestures toward a chart when discussing its central finding.

vocabulary.definition: A presentation that combines two or more modes of communication.
vocabulary.example: A student uses narration, images, and on-screen labels in an explanatory video.

vocabulary.definition: An exchange of questions, responses, and ideas between presenter and audience.
vocabulary.example: After presenting an argument, a student considers and answers a classmate's question.

vocabulary.definition: The oral delivery of a poem, speech, or other text, often from memory.
vocabulary.example: A student recites a selected stanza and explains its imagery and historical context.

vocabulary.definition: Speaking choices that communicate an informed understanding of a text.
vocabulary.example: A student uses pauses and emphasis to clarify the contrast between two ideas in a poem.

vocabulary.definition: Purposeful practice intended to improve content, timing, delivery, or confidence.
vocabulary.example: A presenter records a practice speech and revises the pacing.

suggestedTexts.title: The Gettysburg Address
suggestedTexts.author: Abraham Lincoln
suggestedTexts.purpose: Study concise public speaking, historical context, rhetorical structure, and the delivery of significant language.
suggestedTexts.access: Public domain; use a reputable historical edition.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A brief speech transforms a memorial occasion into a statement of national purpose
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which words and contrasts deserve emphasis during recitation, and how does the historical context inform those decisions?

suggestedTexts.title: Still I Rise
suggestedTexts.author: Maya Angelou
suggestedTexts.purpose: Explore how repetition, direct address, rhythm, and tonal shifts shape the performance of a poem.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed text or authorized recording; verify performance permissions where applicable.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A poem of resilience gains power through repeated declarations
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How might changes in tone, pace, and emphasis communicate the poem's developing argument?

suggestedTexts.title: We Real Cool
suggestedTexts.author: Gwendolyn Brooks
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how line breaks, brevity, sound, and rhythmic ambiguity influence oral interpretation.
suggestedTexts.access: Licensed text or authorized recording.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A remarkably short poem invites sharply different performances
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the placement of pauses change the relationships among the speakers' statements?

suggestedTexts.title: Harlem
suggestedTexts.author: Langston Hughes
suggestedTexts.purpose: Investigate how rhetorical questions, imagery, and sound create possibilities for interpretive recitation.
suggestedTexts.access: Use a licensed or otherwise authorized text.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A series of vivid questions asks what happens when hopes are deferred
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which questions should sound reflective, urgent, or unsettling, and what evidence supports those interpretations?

suggestedTexts.title: The Hill We Climb
suggestedTexts.author: Amanda Gorman
suggestedTexts.purpose: Study how poetic language, sound patterns, gestures, and performance interact with a civic occasion.
suggestedTexts.access: Authorized recording and licensed text; use excerpts within applicable permissions.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A contemporary poet performs a nationally significant work before a broad audience
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the poem's sound patterns and the performer's delivery contribute to its public purpose?

suggestedTexts.title: The Danger of a Single Story
suggestedTexts.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze conversational tone, storytelling, humor, audience engagement, and the relationship between delivery and argument.
suggestedTexts.access: Official TED recording and authorized transcript.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A speaker uses personal experiences to challenge familiar assumptions
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the speaker adapt pacing and tone while moving between anecdotes and broader claims?

suggestedTexts.title: I Have a Dream
suggestedTexts.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how repetition, cadence, historical references, and audience interaction contribute to a major public speech.
suggestedTexts.access: Use an authorized recording or licensed transcript excerpt.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A landmark speech demonstrates the relationship between rhetorical language and oral delivery
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the speaker's delivery reinforce the structure and progression of the argument?

suggestedTexts.title: A Contemporary Student TED-Ed or TEDx Talk
suggestedTexts.author: Selected student or youth speaker
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate how a young speaker organizes ideas, selects supporting media, uses delivery techniques, and addresses an audience.
suggestedTexts.access: Select an official recording appropriate to Grade 9; verify the speaker, topic, and source.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Students analyze a presentation delivered by someone closer to their own age
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which techniques make the presentation effective, and which could be adapted for a classroom audience?

suggestedTexts.title: A Student Literary Research Presentation
suggestedTexts.author: Student researchers
suggestedTexts.purpose: Evaluate how a student explains an interpretation, integrates evidence, uses supporting visuals, and answers questions.
suggestedTexts.access: Use a teacher-created model or an authorized student example.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A model closely resembles the presentation students will create themselves
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What makes the argument easy to follow, and how effectively does the presenter respond to questions?

differentiation.title: Say it so they understand
differentiation.activity: Students prepare a 60–90-second explanation of a familiar topic using a three-part organizer: main idea, supporting detail, and conclusion. They practice with a partner, focusing on clear organization and purposeful pacing. The listener asks one clarification question, and the presenter responds before making one improvement.
differentiation.scaffolds: Presentation organizer, optional speaking notes, teacher model, rehearsal partner, question stems.
differentiation.success: Communicate a clear central idea, include relevant support, make one purposeful delivery choice, and answer an audience question.
differentiation.materials: Planning organizer; speaking notes; simple feedback checklist.

differentiation.title: Poetry in performance
differentiation.activity: Students study a significant poem or excerpt, examining its context, meaning, syntax, sound, and rhetorical choices. They annotate intended pauses, emphasis, and tone, then rehearse and recite all or part of the poem. Afterward, students explain two interpretive delivery decisions and answer a question about the text.
differentiation.scaffolds: Annotated model, historical context notes, audio example, rehearsal opportunities, optional small-group performance.
differentiation.success: Demonstrate accurate understanding of the passage, purposeful interpretive delivery, and the ability to explain choices using textual evidence.
differentiation.materials: Authorized poem or excerpt; annotation sheet; rehearsal and reflection rubric.

differentiation.title: The public humanities talk
differentiation.activity: Students develop a 4–6-minute presentation exploring a meaningful literary or cultural question for an authentic audience. They establish a focused interpretation, research relevant context, integrate appropriate modes, and plan purposeful delivery. Each presentation includes a brief recitation of a significant poem or speech excerpt connected to the topic, followed by audience questions. Students submit a reflection analyzing their content, delivery, and responses.
differentiation.scaffolds: Optional presentation storyboard, source evaluation guide, rehearsal conference, accessibility checklist, question-and-answer planning sheet.
differentiation.success: Deliver a coherent, well-supported, audience-centered presentation with purposeful multimodal choices, informed recitation, effective delivery, and thoughtful audience dialogue.
differentiation.materials: Credible sources; authorized literary excerpt; presentation tools; audience feedback and reflection forms.

questions.prompt: A student must explain a complex scientific process to classmates unfamiliar with the topic. Which presentation strategy best serves the audience?
options: Use technical terminology without explanation.
Speak quickly so every detail fits into the allotted time.
Introduce key terms, organize the process into stages, and use a clearly labeled diagram.
Display a large block of text and read every sentence aloud.
questions.answer: Introduce key terms, organize the process into stages, and use a clearly labeled diagram.
questions.rationale: The strategy supports clear communication and integrates a useful visual mode appropriate to the audience.

questions.prompt: A presenter reaches an especially important conclusion. Which delivery decision is most likely to emphasize it effectively?
options: Maintain the same rapid pace throughout the presentation.
Pause briefly before the conclusion and deliver it at a deliberate pace.
Turn away from the audience and lower the voice until the words are inaudible.
Add unrelated gestures to every word.
questions.answer: Pause briefly before the conclusion and deliver it at a deliberate pace.
questions.rationale: A purposeful pause and controlled pacing can direct audience attention toward an important idea.

questions.prompt: An audience member asks a question that the presenter cannot answer confidently. What is the strongest response?
options: Invent an answer to avoid appearing uncertain.
Ignore the question and immediately end the presentation.
Acknowledge the uncertainty, explain what is known, and identify how the question could be investigated.
Criticize the audience member for asking.
questions.answer: Acknowledge the uncertainty, explain what is known, and identify how the question could be investigated.
questions.rationale: Responsible audience dialogue values accuracy, respectful engagement, and thoughtful responses.

questions.prompt: A student will present the same research findings to classmates and to a school board committee. Explain two ways the presentation might appropriately change while preserving the accuracy of the findings.
questions.answer: A strong response might explain that the student could adjust the amount of background information, examples, terminology, tone, organization, or visual support. Each change should be connected to the needs and purpose of the particular audience.
questions.rationale: Assesses audience-centered choices about clarity, modes, genre, and delivery.

questions.prompt: Select a significant poem or speech excerpt appropriate to Grade 9. Explain its context and central meaning. Annotate the passage to indicate at least three planned delivery choices, such as pauses, emphasis, tone, or pace. Recite the passage and explain how two choices communicate your interpretation.
questions.answer: Evaluate accurate contextual understanding, evidence-based interpretation, preparation, purposeful delivery, and the student's ability to explain how the recitation communicates meaning. Where memory is part of the task, assess it separately from interpretation and delivery.
questions.rationale: Directly addresses the standard's recitation expectation while connecting performance to textual understanding.

questions.prompt: Prepare a 4–6-minute presentation answering a literary or cultural inquiry question. Define your audience and purpose, develop a clear central idea, and support it with evidence from at least two credible sources or relevant texts. Integrate an appropriate visual, audio, or other supporting mode. Include an informed recitation of all or part of a significant poem or speech related to your inquiry. Rehearse tone, pacing, and nonverbal communication. After presenting, ask or invite at least two audience questions and respond thoughtfully. Submit a 300-word reflection evaluating your communication choices, recitation, and audience dialogue.
questions.answer: Evaluate clarity and organization, accuracy and relevance of evidence, appropriateness of presentation modes, purposeful delivery, understanding demonstrated through recitation, responsiveness to questions, and quality of reflection. Provide accessible alternatives for students whose communication needs require them.
questions.rationale: Integrates all five expectations through research-based presentation, multimodal communication, interpretive recitation, audience interaction, and reflection.

evidence: A presentation plan identifying audience, purpose, central idea, and supporting evidence.
A storyboard or outline showing purposeful organization and integration of presentation modes.
An annotated rehearsal script marking tone, pace, emphasis, or nonverbal choices.
A live or recorded presentation demonstrating clear communication.
An annotated significant poem or speech excerpt showing understanding and planned recitation.
A recitation demonstrating interpretive delivery informed by textual analysis.
Audience questions and presenter responses demonstrating thoughtful dialogue.
Peer or teacher feedback identifying specific strengths and improvements.
A self-assessment comparing intended communication effects with audience feedback.
A revision or reflection explaining changes made after rehearsal or presentation.
instruction: Teach presentation as a combination of ideas, audience awareness, format, delivery, and dialogue.
Begin with short, low-stakes speaking opportunities before assigning extended presentations.
Model how to establish a clear central idea and organize information for listeners.
Teach students to select evidence and examples appropriate to their audience's prior knowledge.
Compare presentations from different genres, such as literary readings, research briefings, and persuasive talks.
Demonstrate when visuals, audio, demonstrations, or other modes meaningfully support a message.
Discourage slides filled with text that the presenter simply reads aloud.
Teach tone and pace through comparison of different deliveries of the same short passage.
Use rehearsal recordings or peer observations to help students notice delivery patterns.
Discuss nonverbal communication as context-dependent rather than requiring one universal performance style.
Teach strategies for listening to questions, clarifying their meaning, and responding with evidence.
Model how to acknowledge uncertainty or respectfully address disagreement.
Provide historical and literary context before asking students to recite significant poetry or speeches.
Use close reading and annotation to connect recitation choices with meaning, sound, and rhetorical structure.
Provide students with opportunities to practice, receive feedback, and improve before high-stakes assessment.
Include captions, readable visuals, accessible materials, and appropriate communication accommodations.
Evaluate content, delivery, recitation, and audience dialogue through clearly distinguished criteria.
watchFor: Equating presentation quality with confidence, extroversion, or charisma.
Rewarding volume or theatricality more than clarity and meaning.
Treating eye contact as a universal requirement for effective communication.
Assuming gestures and facial expressions carry identical meanings across cultures and individuals.
Penalizing students for disability-related or language-related differences unrelated to the learning target.
Allowing decorative slides or effects to substitute for accurate content.
Using visuals that are unreadable, unexplained, or inaccessible.
Speaking too quickly to accommodate excessive information.
Assuming slower speech is always better regardless of context.
Memorizing a presentation without understanding its content.
Treating recitation as a memory test disconnected from literary or rhetorical interpretation.
Requiring students to imitate a single supposedly correct performance of a poem.
Selecting significant speeches or poems without teaching their historical or cultural context.
Ignoring copyright or performance permissions when recording or distributing recitations.
Answering audience questions with unsupported claims or invented information.
Treating audience questions as interruptions rather than opportunities for dialogue.
Assessing only the finished presentation without providing opportunities for rehearsal and revision.
Combining all presentation criteria into one vague score that obscures students' strengths and needs.
unpackings.readingSelectionNote: Selections are illustrative teacher-developed recommendations, not state-prescribed works. Confirm access, permissions, excerpt length, age suitability, and any recording or performance restrictions. High Interest and accessibility are editorial judgments rather than validated reading-level measures. Expectation 9.P.CP.2.e explicitly includes recitation of significant poems and speeches; include meaningful recitation in instruction and assessment rather than treating it as optional enrichment. Support varied communication styles and accessibility needs while maintaining the standard's emphasis on purposeful, clear presentation and audience dialogue.

unpackings.status: draft — independently developed instructional guidance; educator review recommended
unpackings.studentFriendly: I can use grammar, usage, and punctuation to communicate clearly and effectively. I can use dashes deliberately to create meaning and emphasis, and I can consult an appropriate style guide when I encounter complicated writing or editing decisions.
know: Standard English conventions support clarity, consistency, credibility, and effective communication.
An em dash can signal an interruption, an abrupt shift, an explanation, an amplification, or emphatic information.
A pair of em dashes can set off an interrupting or parenthetical element within a sentence.
An en dash commonly indicates a range or relationship, depending on the applicable style guide.
A hyphen joins words or word elements and serves a different function from a dash.
Dashes, commas, parentheses, colons, and semicolons have distinct grammatical and rhetorical functions.
A punctuation choice can influence pacing, emphasis, tone, and the relationship between ideas.
Style guides establish conventions for particular disciplines, publications, and communication contexts.
MLA, APA, Chicago, and AP style serve different audiences and purposes.
Style guides may differ in their recommendations about punctuation, capitalization, numbers, abbreviations, and other conventions.
A dictionary, grammar handbook, and style guide serve related but distinct reference functions.
Writers and editors must distinguish between grammatical errors, stylistic preferences, and conventions required by a particular publication or assignment.
Standard English conventions vary across historical periods, genres, and rhetorical situations.
Dialogue, dialect, and deliberate departures from conventional grammar may serve meaningful literary and rhetorical purposes.
understand: Effective writers use conventions to communicate meaning rather than merely to satisfy a checklist of rules.
Punctuation influences how readers interpret relationships between ideas and experience the rhythm of a text.
A dash can create a stronger interruption or emphasis than a comma or parenthesis, but its effectiveness depends on context.
Multiple grammatically acceptable revisions may produce different rhetorical effects.
Consistent adherence to an appropriate style guide supports credibility and readability within a particular discourse community.
Professional writers and editors consult reference resources rather than relying entirely on memory.
A convention that is appropriate in one genre or discipline may be inappropriate in another.
Language choices should be evaluated in relation to audience, purpose, genre, and context.
Editing is an iterative process involving diagnosis, consultation, revision, and evaluation.
Respect for linguistic diversity can coexist with instruction in the conventions expected in formal academic and professional contexts.
do: Identify em dashes, en dashes, and hyphens in authentic texts and explain their distinct functions.
Analyze how an author's use of dashes affects meaning, emphasis, pacing, and tone.
Use a single em dash to introduce an explanation, interruption, amplification, or emphatic conclusion when appropriate.
Use paired em dashes to set off interrupting information while maintaining the grammatical integrity of the surrounding sentence.
Revise sentences using alternative punctuation and explain the effect of each revision.
Identify and correct inappropriate, unnecessary, or inconsistent dash usage.
Distinguish between a grammatically necessary punctuation correction and an optional stylistic revision.
Select an appropriate style guide for an academic, journalistic, literary, or professional writing task.
Locate relevant guidance in a style guide using an index, table of contents, search function, or topic heading.
Apply a style guide's recommendations to resolve complex grammar, usage, or mechanics questions.
Explain and document an editorial decision using evidence from an authoritative reference.
Revise a complete text for clarity, consistency, grammatical accuracy, and rhetorical effectiveness.
Evaluate when unconventional language or punctuation is an intentional and effective authorial choice.
Transfer editing strategies to independent writing across content areas.

vocabulary.definition: An established practice or expectation governing language use in a particular context.
vocabulary.example: Academic writing generally follows conventions for capitalization, punctuation, and sentence structure.

vocabulary.definition: The system governing how words and grammatical structures combine to communicate meaning.
vocabulary.example: Subject-verb agreement is a grammatical convention.

vocabulary.definition: The ways words and expressions are conventionally employed in particular contexts.
vocabulary.example: A writer consults a usage guide to determine whether a disputed expression is appropriate in formal prose.

vocabulary.definition: The written conventions of punctuation, capitalization, spelling, and related formatting.
vocabulary.example: Correct placement of quotation marks is a matter of mechanics.

vocabulary.definition: A long dash used to signal interruption, amplification, explanation, or emphasis.
vocabulary.example: She had one objective—to finish the experiment before sunset.

vocabulary.definition: A dash shorter than an em dash, commonly used to indicate ranges or relationships.
vocabulary.example: Read chapters 4–7.

vocabulary.definition: A short punctuation mark used to join words or word elements.
vocabulary.example: The committee developed a long-term plan.

vocabulary.definition: Supplementary information inserted into a sentence that is not essential to its grammatical structure.
vocabulary.example: The manuscript—lost for nearly a century—was discovered in an archive.

vocabulary.definition: A break in the grammatical or rhetorical flow of a sentence.
vocabulary.example: The answer—if there was an answer—remained uncertain.

vocabulary.definition: The expansion or elaboration of an idea to clarify or emphasize its significance.
vocabulary.example: The storm destroyed everything—the roads, the bridges, and the town's only hospital.

vocabulary.definition: The influence a language choice has on an audience's understanding, emotions, or interpretation.
vocabulary.example: An em dash can create a sudden shift that emphasizes a revelation.

vocabulary.definition: An authoritative reference establishing conventions for writing, editing, and formatting within a particular context.
vocabulary.example: A student consults the MLA Handbook while editing a literary analysis.

vocabulary.definition: The application of the same appropriate conventions throughout a document or publication.
vocabulary.example: An editor checks that dates, abbreviations, and punctuation follow a consistent style.

vocabulary.definition: A group that shares communication practices, purposes, and expectations.
vocabulary.example: Scientists, journalists, and literary scholars belong to discourse communities with different writing conventions.

vocabulary.definition: The level or variety of language appropriate to a particular situation, audience, or purpose.
vocabulary.example: A research report generally uses a more formal register than a conversation between friends.

vocabulary.definition: The process of reviewing written material for accuracy, clarity, consistency, grammar, usage, and mechanics.
vocabulary.example: A copyeditor checks a magazine article against the publication's style guide.

targets: I can distinguish among em dashes, en dashes, and hyphens.
I can explain why an author uses a dash instead of another punctuation mark.
I can use a single em dash to create an effective interruption, explanation, or emphasis.
I can use paired em dashes to set off supplementary information.
I can revise punctuation to create a deliberate rhetorical effect.
I can identify the style guide appropriate to a particular writing situation.
I can locate and interpret guidance about a complex writing or editing question.
I can justify an editorial decision using an authoritative reference.
I can distinguish between grammatical errors and intentional stylistic choices.
I can independently edit my writing for clarity, accuracy, and consistency.

suggestedTexts.title: Because I could not stop for Death
suggestedTexts.author: Emily Dickinson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how dashes influence rhythm, interruption, ambiguity, and the reader's experience of time.

suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; short text with figurative language and unconventional punctuation.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How would replacing Dickinson's dashes with conventional punctuation change the poem's pacing and meaning?

suggestedTexts.title: The Tell-Tale Heart
suggestedTexts.author: Edgar Allan Poe
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how punctuation, repetition, and interruptions contribute to an unreliable narrator's emotional intensity.
suggestedTexts.access: Public domain; available through Project Gutenberg and other established literary archives.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; suspenseful narrative with some nineteenth-century vocabulary.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A narrator insists on being sane while describing increasingly disturbing behavior.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which punctuation choices help create the narrator's frantic voice, and what would be lost if the passage were conventionally punctuated?

suggestedTexts.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how interruptions, elaboration, and carefully structured sentences contribute to the development of an argument.
suggestedTexts.access: Use an authorized edition or a school-licensed anthology; copyright and reproduction permissions apply.

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do punctuation and sentence structure help the writer clarify complex relationships between ideas?

suggestedTexts.title: The House on Mango Street
suggestedTexts.author: Sandra Cisneros
suggestedTexts.purpose: Distinguish intentional literary departures from formal conventions from errors that interfere with communication.
suggestedTexts.access: School library, licensed ebook, or purchased edition.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible prose with layered literary and cultural meaning.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Short, vivid accounts of identity, belonging, family, and neighborhood life.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the author's sentence structures and punctuation contribute to the narrator's distinctive voice?

suggestedTexts.title: The Danger of a Single Story
suggestedTexts.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare the punctuation of a published transcript with the speaker's pauses, shifts, and emphasis.
suggestedTexts.access: Official TED talk and transcript; consult applicable terms of use.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible spoken language with important cultural and rhetorical complexity.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How can an editor represent a speaker's interruptions and changes in emphasis without distorting the original meaning?

suggestedTexts.title: The Case for Reparations
suggestedTexts.author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how editorial conventions and sentence-level choices support clarity in a complex argument.
suggestedTexts.access: Published by The Atlantic; use an authorized excerpt or available institutional subscription.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Advanced; requires historical and contextual scaffolding.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the writer manage supplementary information while maintaining the momentum of the central argument?

suggestedTexts.title: The Punctuation Guide
suggestedTexts.author: Jordan Penn
suggestedTexts.purpose: Consult explanations and examples of em dashes, en dashes, and hyphens while solving authentic editing problems.
suggestedTexts.access: https://www.thepunctuationguide.com/
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible reference text with concise examples.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: Which punctuation mark best communicates the intended relationship between these ideas?

suggestedTexts.title: MLA Handbook
suggestedTexts.author: Modern Language Association
suggestedTexts.purpose: Locate and apply conventions appropriate to humanities research and literary analysis.

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How might the conventions appropriate to a psychology research report differ from those used in a literary analysis?

suggestedTexts.purpose: Investigate complex punctuation and usage questions and examine the role of editorial judgment.

suggestedTexts.accessibility: Advanced reference resource; provide specific lookup tasks.

suggestedTexts.title: AP Stylebook
suggestedTexts.author: Associated Press
suggestedTexts.purpose: Explore conventions appropriate to journalism and compare them with academic writing conventions.
