differentiation.title: Three marks, three jobs
differentiation.activity: Students sort authentic and teacher-created examples into em dash, en dash, and hyphen categories. They identify the relationship communicated by each mark and correct examples in which the marks have been confused. Students finish by composing one original example of each.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide color-coded punctuation marks, annotated examples, a reference chart, and sentence frames explaining the function of each mark.
differentiation.success: Students correctly classify at least eight of ten examples and produce three original sentences demonstrating the distinct functions of the punctuation marks.

differentiation.title: Build the interrupted sentence
differentiation.activity: Students begin with a complete sentence and identify its subject and predicate. They insert a supplementary phrase using paired em dashes, then remove the phrase to verify that the original sentence remains grammatically complete. Students revise examples containing misplaced or unmatched dashes.
differentiation.scaffolds: Model the process with a think-aloud. Underline the sentence's essential grammatical structure and place brackets around supplementary information before adding punctuation.
differentiation.success: Students correctly construct and revise four of five sentences containing paired em dashes and explain why the surrounding sentence remains complete.

differentiation.title: Find the answer, not the guess
differentiation.activity: Students receive a short list of editing questions and a teacher-selected style guide. They practice identifying keywords, navigating the reference, locating relevant guidance, and recording the recommendation in their own words. Students apply the guidance to a sample sentence.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide suggested search terms, section headings, a partially completed model, and guided practice before independent consultation.
differentiation.success: Students locate appropriate guidance for three editorial questions and correctly apply the recommendation to at least two sample sentences.

differentiation.title: Punctuation changes the meaning
differentiation.activity: Students examine sentences from literary and informational mentor texts. They create alternative versions using commas, parentheses, colons, or em dashes where grammatically appropriate. In a short analytical response, students compare the effects of the revisions on pacing, emphasis, tone, and clarity.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide an initial modeled comparison and a vocabulary bank containing interruption, amplification, emphasis, and parenthetical information.
differentiation.success: Students produce three grammatically defensible revisions and explain the rhetorical effect of each punctuation choice using specific evidence.

differentiation.title: The editorial desk
differentiation.activity: Students act as copyeditors for a school publication. They receive a draft containing complex punctuation, capitalization, abbreviation, and usage decisions. Using a designated style guide, they identify issues, revise the draft, and create an editorial decision log explaining the guidance behind each substantive change.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide a model editorial decision that identifies the issue, cites the reference location, explains the recommendation, and presents the revision.
differentiation.success: Students resolve at least five editorial issues accurately and document the reasoning and reference guidance supporting their decisions.

differentiation.title: Author's punctuation fingerprint
differentiation.activity: Students examine a passage from Emily Dickinson, Edgar Allan Poe, or another teacher-selected author. They annotate recurring punctuation patterns and explain how those patterns contribute to the author's voice. Students then write a short original passage that uses a similar punctuation strategy for a different purpose.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide a short list of possible rhetorical effects and model how to connect a punctuation choice to a specific interpretation.
differentiation.success: Students support an interpretation with at least three textual examples and use a comparable punctuation strategy effectively in their own writing.

differentiation.title: Edit your own argument
differentiation.activity: Students revisit an argumentative essay or research-based paragraph. They identify places where punctuation or usage affects clarity, consult an appropriate reference, and make purposeful revisions. Students submit the original passage, revised passage, and a brief reflection explaining their editorial decisions.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide a checklist emphasizing sentence boundaries, supplementary information, consistency, and punctuation choices that support the argument.
differentiation.success: Students make at least three substantive, justified revisions that improve clarity, accuracy, or rhetorical effectiveness.

differentiation.title: One story, three editorial styles
differentiation.activity: Students adapt a short informational text for three different contexts: a school newspaper, a humanities publication, and a social-science report. They consult appropriate style resources, identify meaningful differences in conventions, and create an editorial rationale explaining how their revisions respond to each audience and purpose.
materials: AP Stylebook or teacher-provided authorized guidance
differentiation.scaffolds: Offer a comparison matrix but require students to independently identify and investigate the editorial questions.
differentiation.success: Students produce three internally consistent versions and accurately explain at least four context-specific editorial decisions using authoritative references.

differentiation.title: The intentional rule-breaker
differentiation.activity: Students investigate an author whose punctuation or syntax departs from conventional formal prose. They analyze the relationship between the unconventional choices and the text's voice, genre, and meaning. Students write a critical editorial memo distinguishing deliberate stylistic decisions from changes that would improve readability without erasing the author's voice.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide guiding questions about voice, audience, linguistic diversity, historical context, and the limits of editorial intervention.
differentiation.success: Students construct a nuanced argument supported by textual evidence and explain which features should be preserved, revised, or evaluated according to context.

differentiation.title: Create a publication style sheet
differentiation.activity: Students develop a concise editorial style sheet for a school literary magazine, research journal, or student newspaper. They select an appropriate governing style guide, identify recurring editorial decisions, create examples, and explain how the style sheet will promote consistency while respecting authorial voice.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide examples of editorial style sheets and require students to distinguish established reference guidance from publication-specific preferences.
differentiation.success: Students create a usable style sheet containing at least eight accurate conventions, illustrative examples, and a clear rationale for the selected editorial approach.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an em dash appropriately to introduce an emphatic explanation?
options: The students read pages 12—18 before class.
The committee faced one major obstacle—a lack of reliable funding.
The committee developed a long—term strategy.
The students—submitted their assignments on Friday.
questions.answer: B
questions.rationale: The em dash introduces an explanation of the major obstacle. Option A uses an em dash for a numerical range, option C substitutes a dash for a hyphen, and option D unnecessarily interrupts the subject and predicate.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly uses paired em dashes to set off supplementary information?
options: The exhibition—originally scheduled for May—opened in June.
The exhibition—originally scheduled for May, opened in June.
The exhibition originally—scheduled for May opened—in June.
The exhibition—opened in June—because.
questions.answer: A
questions.rationale: The paired dashes enclose a supplementary phrase. Removing the phrase leaves the complete sentence: The exhibition opened in June.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the rhetorical effect of the dash in the sentence: The hikers expected a difficult journey—but nothing could have prepared them for the storm.
options: It joins two words into a compound adjective.
It introduces a numerical range.
It creates an emphatic shift from expectation to unexpected reality.
It indicates that the sentence contains a quotation.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: The dash emphasizes the contrast between what the hikers expected and the severity of what they experienced.

questions.prompt: Which punctuation mark is conventionally appropriate for indicating a range of years in a style that uses en dashes for ranges?
options: Em dash
En dash
Apostrophe
Semicolon
questions.answer: B
questions.rationale: An en dash commonly indicates a range, such as 1914–1918. Writers should follow the applicable style guide.

questions.prompt: A student is preparing a literary analysis for an English class that requires MLA style. Which resource is most appropriate for resolving a complex question about the assignment's editorial conventions?
options: The MLA Handbook
The AP Stylebook
A social media discussion
An unverified grammar correction website
questions.answer: A
questions.rationale: The assignment explicitly requires MLA style, making the MLA Handbook the appropriate governing reference.

questions.prompt: Two style guides recommend different conventions for the same punctuation issue. What should a writer do first?
options: Assume that the newer guide is always correct.
Choose whichever recommendation requires less editing.
Identify which style guide governs the intended publication or assignment.
Avoid using the punctuation mark altogether.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: Editorial conventions depend on context. The writer should first establish which reference applies to the intended audience and publication.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between grammar and style?
options: Every stylistic preference is a universal grammatical rule.
Grammar concerns language structure, while style includes choices shaped by context, purpose, and editorial conventions.
Style applies only to fictional writing.
Grammar and style are unrelated to meaning.
questions.answer: B
questions.rationale: Grammar and style are related but distinct. Multiple grammatically acceptable constructions may be evaluated differently according to rhetorical purpose or editorial expectations.

questions.prompt: Revise the following sentence to correct its punctuation: The researcher originally trained as a chemist—developed a new method for analyzing the samples.
questions.answer: One acceptable revision is: The researcher—originally trained as a chemist—developed a new method for analyzing the samples.
questions.rationale: The supplementary phrase requires a matching opening dash if paired em dashes are used. The essential sentence is The researcher developed a new method for analyzing the samples.

questions.prompt: Revise the sentence using appropriate punctuation for both the compound modifier and the numerical range: The students completed a three—week project covering chapters 5—9.
questions.answer: The students completed a three-week project covering chapters 5–9.
questions.rationale: The hyphen joins the compound modifier three-week. An en dash indicates the chapter range under conventions that use en dashes for ranges.

questions.prompt: Compare these sentences: The answer, surprisingly, was correct. The answer—surprisingly—was correct. Explain how the punctuation changes the reader's experience.
questions.answer: Both sentences are grammatically acceptable. The commas integrate the supplementary word more smoothly into the sentence, while the paired em dashes create a stronger interruption and emphasize the speaker's surprise.
questions.rationale: A complete response identifies the supplementary element and explains a meaningful difference in pacing or emphasis.

questions.prompt: Explain why a writer might use an em dash rather than a colon to introduce an explanation.
questions.answer: An em dash can introduce an explanation with a stronger sense of interruption, immediacy, or emphasis. A colon often creates a more formal or anticipated relationship between a complete introductory clause and the explanation. The most effective choice depends on the sentence structure and rhetorical purpose.
questions.rationale: Students should explain a contextual difference rather than claim that the two marks are always interchangeable.

questions.prompt: An editor notices that a poet repeatedly uses unconventional punctuation. Explain why automatically correcting every instance may be inappropriate.
questions.answer: Unconventional punctuation may be an intentional artistic choice that shapes rhythm, voice, ambiguity, or meaning. An editor should examine the genre, historical context, authorial purpose, and publication requirements before making changes.
questions.rationale: Students should distinguish deliberate stylistic choices from errors and explain the importance of context.

questions.prompt: Your school newspaper has adopted AP style. Locate guidance in an appropriate reference about dash usage or another teacher-assigned mechanics question. Record the reference location, summarize the recommendation, and apply it to a sample sentence.
questions.answer: Responses will vary according to the selected question and edition of the reference. A successful response identifies the governing guide, accurately locates and paraphrases the relevant recommendation, and applies it correctly.
questions.rationale: This task assesses independent consultation and application rather than memorization of a particular style rule.

questions.prompt: Investigate a complex editorial question using two authoritative style guides. Explain whether their recommendations differ and identify which recommendation should govern a particular writing task.
questions.answer: Responses should accurately represent both references, identify any meaningful differences or similarities, and justify the applicable recommendation using the assignment's audience, purpose, discipline, or publication requirements.
questions.rationale: Students demonstrate that editorial conventions are contextual and that authoritative references must be selected deliberately.

questions.prompt: Analyze how an author uses dashes and other punctuation in a selected literary or informational passage. Explain how these choices influence meaning, pacing, emphasis, or voice. Include at least three specific textual examples.
questions.answer: A strong response develops a defensible interpretation, accurately identifies punctuation functions, connects specific examples to rhetorical effects, and explains how the choices contribute to the passage's larger purpose.
questions.rationale: Score the accuracy of grammatical analysis, relevance of textual evidence, depth of rhetorical interpretation, and clarity of explanation.

questions.prompt: Edit a complete student-written or teacher-provided article for publication. Resolve complex grammar, usage, and mechanics questions using an appropriate style guide. Submit the original draft, revised draft, and an editorial decision log.
questions.answer: Successful work demonstrates accurate and purposeful revisions, consistent application of the designated style, reliable reference consultation, and clear explanations of substantive editorial decisions.
questions.rationale: Evaluate the quality of revisions, accuracy of reference use, consistency, rhetorical effectiveness, and independence.

unpackings.studentFriendly: I can compare how different authors and speakers present the same topic, explain how their experiences and circumstances influence their perspectives, recognize commercial influences in digital media, and combine information from credible sources to develop my own understanding of a question.
know: Perspective is the position or lens through which an author or speaker understands and presents a subject.
An author's perspective may be influenced by personal experiences, cultural background, historical circumstances, disciplinary knowledge, values, and intended audience.
Perspective is communicated through selection of details, diction, tone, organization, examples, evidence, imagery, and rhetorical choices.
Authors and speakers may present the same topic differently because they have different experiences, purposes, audiences, or assumptions.
Perspective, point of view, bias, purpose, and tone are related but distinct concepts.
A perspective may be explicitly stated or implicitly developed through patterns of language and evidence.
Authors can shape readers' perceptions by emphasizing particular information, omitting other information, or framing events in specific ways.
Framing involves presenting information through a particular interpretive lens.
Commercial influences include advertisements, sponsorships, affiliate marketing, product placement, paid endorsements, branded content, and other financial relationships.
Digital and audiovisual texts may combine informational, entertainment, persuasive, and commercial purposes.
Commercial influence does not automatically make information false, but it creates a reason to examine the text's purpose, evidence, and credibility.
Historical context includes the events, conditions, beliefs, institutions, and social structures surrounding the creation of a text.
Disciplinary context includes the methods, assumptions, vocabulary, evidence standards, and questions associated with a field of study.
Perspectives can change across time as societies, knowledge, technologies, institutions, and cultural expectations change.
Texts about the same subject may reflect different disciplinary perspectives, such as historical, scientific, economic, ethical, or literary perspectives.
Credible sources demonstrate relevant expertise, transparent evidence, appropriate methods, accuracy, and accountability.
Source credibility must be evaluated in relation to the particular research question and claim.
Synthesis combines information and perspectives from multiple sources to develop a coherent understanding, explanation, or argument.
Synthesis differs from summarizing sources individually because it identifies relationships among ideas.
Effective synthesis may identify agreement, disagreement, qualification, causation, gaps, and patterns across sources.
Responsible research distinguishes between source information, interpretation, and the researcher's own conclusions.
Attribution allows readers to identify the origins of information and evaluate how sources contribute to a text.
understand: Texts are created by people working within particular circumstances rather than emerging independently of historical, cultural, disciplinary, or personal contexts.
An author's perspective shapes both what a text communicates and how that information is presented.
Different perspectives on a shared topic can reveal assumptions, priorities, experiences, and interpretations that might otherwise remain invisible.
Analyzing perspective requires evidence from the text rather than speculation about an author's personal beliefs or identity.
Readers should distinguish between an author's demonstrated perspective and assumptions they make about the author.
The same evidence can be interpreted differently when authors approach a subject through different disciplinary frameworks or purposes.
A text's framing can influence what readers consider important, credible, normal, problematic, or desirable.
Commercial relationships can influence the selection, presentation, emphasis, and distribution of information.
Recognizing commercial influence helps readers make informed judgments without automatically dismissing sponsored or advertising-supported content.
Historical understanding can clarify why a perspective was developed and how its meaning or reception changes over time.
Comparing texts across historical periods can reveal continuity, change, disagreement, and evolving social assumptions.
Disciplinary perspectives contribute different kinds of evidence and explanations to complex questions.
Credibility is not identical to agreement with a reader's existing beliefs.

Synthesis creates new understanding by connecting ideas across sources while accurately representing their differences.

vocabulary.definition: The position, experience, or interpretive lens through which a person understands and presents a subject.
vocabulary.example: A physician and a patient may present different perspectives on the same healthcare policy.

vocabulary.definition: The position from which a narrative is told or a subject is presented.
vocabulary.example: A first-person narrator presents events through personal observations and experiences.

vocabulary.definition: The position or attitude an author communicates toward a subject through explicit statements and rhetorical choices.
vocabulary.example: An essayist communicates skepticism toward a proposed policy through carefully selected evidence and qualifying language.

vocabulary.definition: The presentation of information through a particular interpretive lens that emphasizes certain aspects of a subject.
vocabulary.example: One article frames artificial intelligence as an economic opportunity, while another frames it as a labor concern.

vocabulary.definition: A tendency or inclination that can influence the selection, interpretation, or presentation of information.
vocabulary.example: A report may demonstrate selection bias if it relies only on evidence supporting its preferred conclusion.

vocabulary.definition: An idea accepted as true without being explicitly established within a particular text.
vocabulary.example: An argument about transportation may assume that every household has access to a car.

vocabulary.definition: The attitude communicated toward a subject or audience through language and rhetorical choices.
vocabulary.example: An editorial may communicate an urgent, skeptical, or optimistic tone.

vocabulary.definition: A deliberate decision about language, structure, evidence, or presentation intended to influence communication.
vocabulary.example: An author begins an argument with a personal story to make an abstract issue more immediate.

vocabulary.definition: The decision to give particular information greater attention or importance than other information.
vocabulary.example: Two reports about a new development may emphasize either job creation or environmental effects.

vocabulary.definition: The historical circumstances, events, institutions, beliefs, and social conditions surrounding a text's creation.
vocabulary.example: Understanding segregation helps readers interpret the arguments in Letter from Birmingham Jail.

vocabulary.definition: The methods, assumptions, vocabulary, evidence standards, and purposes associated with a field of study.
vocabulary.example: A historian and a climate scientist may investigate the same environmental event using different methods and evidence.

vocabulary.definition: The influence of financial relationships or business interests on the creation, presentation, or distribution of a text.
vocabulary.example: A sponsored product review may emphasize features that are important to the sponsoring company.

vocabulary.definition: Content produced or distributed with financial support from an advertiser or sponsor.
vocabulary.example: A travel article labeled as a paid partnership may have been funded by a tourism organization.

vocabulary.definition: Advertising designed to resemble the format and style of surrounding editorial or informational content.
vocabulary.example: An advertisement appears in the same visual format as news articles but includes a sponsored-content label.

vocabulary.definition: A commercial arrangement in which a person or organization may receive compensation when an audience member makes a purchase through a designated link.
vocabulary.example: A technology reviewer discloses that purchases made through links in the video description may generate commissions.

vocabulary.definition: The inclusion of a product or brand within entertainment or informational content, sometimes through a commercial arrangement.
vocabulary.example: A character prominently uses a particular brand of phone in a film.

vocabulary.definition: A statement revealing a relevant relationship, interest, limitation, or commercial arrangement.
vocabulary.example: A creator identifies a video as a paid partnership with a company.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which a source or claim deserves trust based on relevant expertise, evidence, methods, and accountability.
vocabulary.example: A peer-reviewed scientific study may provide credible evidence about a specific scientific question.

vocabulary.definition: The process of checking information against additional independent evidence or sources.
vocabulary.example: A researcher compares a historical claim with archival documents and scholarly research.

vocabulary.definition: The integration of information and ideas from multiple sources to develop a coherent understanding or argument.
vocabulary.example: A student combines scientific research, historical evidence, and economic analysis to explain the effects of urban development.

vocabulary.definition: A limitation or condition that makes a claim more precise and appropriately cautious.
vocabulary.example: The evidence suggests that the program improved outcomes for some participants, although its long-term effects remain uncertain.

vocabulary.definition: The identification of the source responsible for information, language, or an idea.
vocabulary.example: A researcher names the organization responsible for a statistical finding.

vocabulary.definition: Evaluating a source by consulting independent information about its author, organization, claims, or reputation.
vocabulary.example: A student opens additional sources to investigate the organization publishing an unfamiliar report.

vocabulary.definition: A group that shares communication practices, purposes, specialized vocabulary, and expectations for evidence.
vocabulary.example: Historians and medical researchers belong to different discourse communities.

suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does King represent the perspectives of his critics, and how does his response reveal the historical circumstances shaping his argument?

suggestedTexts.title: A Call for Unity
suggestedTexts.author: Eight Alabama clergymen
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare the perspective and framing of the clergymen's statement with King's response in Letter from Birmingham Jail.
suggestedTexts.access: Consult historical archives, authorized educational resources, or licensed collections for the text.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the clergymen and King frame the same demonstrations differently, and what assumptions underlie their arguments?

suggestedTexts.title: Ain't I a Woman?
suggestedTexts.author: Sojourner Truth
suggestedTexts.genre: Speech as preserved in historical accounts
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare historical accounts of a speech and examine how transcription, publication, and historical context influence the representation of a speaker's perspective.
suggestedTexts.access: Public-domain historical accounts; compare the 1851 Marius Robinson account and the 1863 Frances Dana Gage version through reliable historical resources.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; provide context about abolition, women's rights, and the reliability of historical accounts.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Two substantially different published accounts preserve a famous speech, raising questions about whose words readers encounter.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the differences between the published accounts affect readers' perceptions of Truth, and what should a responsible researcher conclude about their reliability?

suggestedTexts.title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
suggestedTexts.author: Frederick Douglass
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how historical circumstances and rhetorical choices influence a speaker's perspective on national identity, liberty, and citizenship.
suggestedTexts.access: Public domain; available through established historical and literary archives.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Advanced; provide historical context and support for nineteenth-century rhetorical language.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does Douglass use contrasting perspectives on Independence Day to challenge the beliefs of his audience?

suggestedTexts.title: Declaration of Independence
suggestedTexts.author: Continental Congress; principal draft by Thomas Jefferson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare historical perspectives on liberty, equality, and political authority with later texts that challenge or extend the document's claims.
suggestedTexts.access: Public domain; available through the National Archives.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the historical circumstances of the document influence its claims, and how do later authors reinterpret those claims?

suggestedTexts.title: Shooting an Elephant
suggestedTexts.author: George Orwell
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how personal experience, colonial circumstances, and retrospective interpretation shape an author's perspective.
suggestedTexts.access: Use a licensed anthology or an edition available through the school library; copyright status varies by jurisdiction.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate to advanced; contextualize British imperialism and the essay's treatment of violence.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: An official faces a decision shaped by public pressure, personal conscience, and imperial authority.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does Orwell's presentation of his experience reveal tensions between personal judgment and institutional power?

suggestedTexts.title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
suggestedTexts.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare ethical perspectives on collective prosperity, individual suffering, responsibility, and social arrangements.
suggestedTexts.access: School library, licensed anthology, or purchased edition.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; abstract ethical questions and potentially disturbing subject matter.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A seemingly ideal society depends on a disturbing moral compromise.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does the narrator's framing of the city influence the reader's ethical judgment, and how might different philosophical perspectives interpret the story?

suggestedTexts.title: The Case for Reparations
suggestedTexts.author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how historical evidence, personal narratives, and economic context contribute to an author's perspective on public policy.
suggestedTexts.access: Published by The Atlantic; use an authorized excerpt or institutional subscription.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Advanced; requires historical and economic background.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does Coates combine individual experiences and historical evidence to shape readers' understanding of a contemporary issue?

suggestedTexts.title: Silent Spring
suggestedTexts.author: Rachel Carson
suggestedTexts.purpose: Examine how scientific evidence, literary techniques, and historical circumstances shape a perspective on environmental risk.
suggestedTexts.access: School library, licensed ebook, or purchased edition.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate to advanced; provide scientific and historical context.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A scientist and writer challenges widely accepted practices by examining their environmental consequences.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How does Carson combine scientific and literary approaches to influence public understanding of environmental problems?

suggestedTexts.title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
suggestedTexts.author: Rebecca Skloot
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare scientific, historical, personal, and ethical perspectives on medical research and informed consent.
suggestedTexts.access: School library, licensed ebook, or purchased edition.
suggestedTexts.readingTime: 20–30 minutes for a selected chapter or excerpt
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Moderate; provide background on cell research and medical ethics.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: A woman's cells transform modern medicine while her family confronts questions about consent, recognition, and justice.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do scientific, medical, historical, and family perspectives contribute different kinds of understanding to the same events?

suggestedTexts.title: The Story of an Hour
suggestedTexts.author: Kate Chopin
suggestedTexts.purpose: Analyze how historical context and narrative perspective influence interpretations of marriage, independence, and social expectations.
suggestedTexts.access: Public domain; available through established literary archives.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Unexpected news leads a woman to imagine a future radically different from the life she has known.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the story's historical circumstances influence its treatment of independence, and how might readers from different periods interpret the ending?

suggestedTexts.title: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
suggestedTexts.author: Federal Trade Commission
suggestedTexts.purpose: Identify overt commercial relationships and examine how disclosures help audiences interpret digital endorsements.
suggestedTexts.access: Publicly available through https://www.ftc.gov/
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible practical guidance with concrete examples.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Students investigate when social media creators should disclose relationships with companies whose products they recommend.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What commercial relationships should audiences be able to recognize, and how might disclosure change the interpretation of an endorsement?

suggestedTexts.title: Teacher-selected sponsored and independent product reviews
suggestedTexts.author: Various digital creators and publishers
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare how disclosed commercial relationships may influence product presentation, evidence, and audience expectations.
suggestedTexts.access: Select current, age-appropriate examples from publicly accessible videos or articles. Verify sponsorship labels and avoid assuming undisclosed financial relationships.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Accessible; provide captions or transcripts when available.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Students investigate whether a review is primarily informing an audience, selling a product, or doing both.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: What evidence identifies a commercial influence, and how does the review's presentation differ from an independently produced comparison?

suggestedTexts.title: Teacher-selected interdisciplinary source set on artificial intelligence
suggestedTexts.author: Various researchers, educators, journalists, and organizations
suggestedTexts.genre: Research articles, reports, journalism, and commentary
suggestedTexts.purpose: Compare educational, economic, technological, ethical, and commercial perspectives while synthesizing credible information.
suggestedTexts.access: Select current sources through school library databases, government publications, university research, and reputable journalism. Verify dates, evidence, and commercial disclosures.
suggestedTexts.accessibility: Variable; use a combination of accessible reporting and appropriately scaffolded research.
suggestedTexts.interestHook: Students investigate a technology that directly affects their learning, future careers, and everyday lives.
suggestedTexts.teachingPrompt: How do the authors' disciplinary contexts and institutional interests shape their perspectives, and what conclusions can be supported across the sources?

differentiation.title: Same topic, different lens
differentiation.activity: Students read two short passages presenting different perspectives on a familiar topic such as school uniforms, homework, or public transportation. They highlight words and details that reveal each perspective, then complete a comparison organizer identifying the shared topic, each author's position, and supporting evidence.
materials: Two accessible passages on a shared topic
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide sentence frames such as Both authors discuss..., Author A emphasizes..., and This wording suggests.... Model the distinction between identifying a topic and identifying a perspective.
differentiation.success: Students accurately identify both perspectives, support each interpretation with at least two textual details, and explain one meaningful difference.

differentiation.title: Spot the commercial signal
differentiation.activity: Students examine teacher-selected screenshots of advertisements, sponsored posts, affiliate disclosures, and independent informational content. They identify visible commercial signals and explain what those signals reveal about the text's purpose or financial relationships.
differentiation.scaffolds: Teach common disclosure language and provide examples of sponsorship labels, affiliate notices, advertisements, and product placement. Distinguish confirmed commercial evidence from speculation.
differentiation.success: Students correctly identify overt commercial signals in at least four of five examples and explain why each signal matters to an audience.

differentiation.title: Context clues beyond the text
differentiation.activity: Students read a short historical text and receive a concise timeline, author background, and explanation of relevant historical circumstances. They match textual details with contextual information and explain how the context helps clarify the author's perspective.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide selected contextual facts, model one evidence-based connection, and use guiding questions about when, where, why, and for whom the text was created.
differentiation.success: Students make at least three accurate connections between contextual information and specific features of the text.

differentiation.title: From two summaries to one synthesis
differentiation.activity: Students read two short credible sources addressing a focused question. After identifying the central idea of each source, they sort information into shared findings, differences, and unanswered questions. They use the organizer to write a paragraph that combines information from both sources.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide a completed example, transition phrases for agreement and contrast, and attribution sentence frames. Highlight how synthesis organizes ideas by relationship rather than by source.
differentiation.success: Students produce a coherent paragraph that accurately integrates information from both sources and identifies at least one relationship between their ideas.

differentiation.title: Framing the same event
differentiation.activity: Students compare three credible texts covering the same event or issue. They analyze headlines, introductory paragraphs, selected evidence, quotations, images, and language choices. Students identify how each text establishes perspective and write an evidence-based explanation of how framing may influence audience perceptions.
materials: Three current or historical texts on a shared topic
differentiation.scaffolds: Model a comparison of two headlines and provide categories for diction, emphasis, evidence, organization, and omissions. Require students to distinguish documented differences from assumptions about motives.
differentiation.success: Students accurately compare all three perspectives and explain at least three specific rhetorical choices that influence audience interpretation.

differentiation.title: Who paid for this message?
differentiation.activity: Students compare a disclosed sponsored video or article with an independently produced text addressing a similar product, destination, or issue. They identify commercial disclosures, analyze presentation choices, examine evidence, and evaluate what audiences should consider when interpreting the texts.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide a checklist covering sponsorship, affiliate relationships, advertisements, product placement, evidence, and missing information. Emphasize that commercial influence does not automatically establish inaccuracy.
differentiation.success: Students identify verified commercial influences, explain how at least two presentation choices may relate to those influences, and support a nuanced evaluation with evidence.

differentiation.title: A historical conversation
differentiation.activity: Students compare selected passages from the Declaration of Independence, Frederick Douglass's What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?, and Martin Luther King Jr.'s Letter from Birmingham Jail. They investigate the historical circumstances surrounding each text and analyze how the authors develop perspectives on liberty, equality, and citizenship across time.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide brief contextual readings, define unfamiliar historical vocabulary, and model how to connect a specific rhetorical choice to a documented historical circumstance.
differentiation.success: Students develop a comparative analysis that accurately represents all three texts and explains how historical contexts influence their perspectives and rhetorical choices.

differentiation.title: One issue, three disciplines
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a shared issue such as climate change, artificial intelligence, public health, or urban development through sources representing three disciplines. They identify each discipline's central questions, methods, evidence, vocabulary, and perspective, then explain how these differences shape the resulting texts.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide an introductory explanation of disciplinary perspectives and examples of how historians, scientists, economists, and ethicists investigate different aspects of a problem.
differentiation.success: Students accurately identify the approaches of three disciplines and explain how their methods and purposes influence the perspectives presented in the sources.

differentiation.title: The synthesis investigation
differentiation.activity: Students develop a focused question about an academic topic or personal interest. They locate at least four credible sources representing relevant perspectives, evaluate each source, organize information by themes, and compose an explanatory synthesis that addresses the research question.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide sample research questions, a modeled synthesis paragraph, and a matrix for recording agreements, disagreements, evidence, and limitations. Offer teacher or librarian conferences during source selection.
differentiation.success: Students integrate at least four credible sources into a coherent response, accurately represent their relationships, provide appropriate attribution, and develop a conclusion supported by the available evidence.

differentiation.title: The author's choices
differentiation.activity: Students analyze a speech or essay and identify how the author establishes perspective through personal experience, diction, tone, selected examples, and organization. They then rewrite a short passage from a different defensible perspective and explain the rhetorical decisions made during revision.
differentiation.scaffolds: Model a change in framing while preserving factual accuracy. Provide reminders that adopting another perspective does not justify inventing evidence or misrepresenting people.
differentiation.success: Students support their original analysis with textual evidence and create a revised passage that establishes a distinct perspective through deliberate rhetorical choices.

differentiation.title: Whose words are we reading?
differentiation.activity: Students investigate the 1851 and 1863 published accounts of Sojourner Truth's famous speech. They research the circumstances of each account, compare differences in language and presentation, examine the limitations of historical evidence, and write an analysis explaining how transcription and publication can influence the representation of a speaker's perspective.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide guidance on distinguishing primary sources, later recollections, historical interpretation, and unsupported claims. Encourage students to acknowledge uncertainty rather than assume either account is a verbatim transcript.
differentiation.success: Students produce a nuanced analysis supported by both accounts and credible historical research, accurately explaining differences, contextual influences, and limitations.

differentiation.title: Investigate the influence economy
differentiation.activity: Students research a selected form of digital commercial communication such as influencer marketing, sponsored journalism, affiliate reviews, or branded entertainment. They examine examples, consult credible consumer guidance and research, and create an analytical report explaining how commercial relationships can shape content and audience interpretation.
materials: Credible research on advertising or media
differentiation.scaffolds: Require students to distinguish disclosed financial relationships from inferred motives and to evaluate the accuracy of claims independently of commercial status.
differentiation.success: Students synthesize evidence from multiple credible sources, accurately identify overt commercial influences, and explain how specific media choices affect audiences without making unsupported accusations.

differentiation.title: The interdisciplinary briefing
differentiation.activity: Students investigate a complex issue through historical, scientific, economic, ethical, and cultural perspectives as appropriate. They create a briefing that identifies each disciplinary contribution, explains disagreements or limitations, synthesizes credible findings, and recommends additional questions for investigation.
differentiation.scaffolds: Provide a model policy or research briefing and require students to evaluate the relevance of each discipline rather than include perspectives simply to meet a numerical requirement.
differentiation.success: Students produce a coherent, evidence-based briefing that integrates at least five credible sources, accurately explains disciplinary differences, and acknowledges meaningful uncertainty or limitations.

differentiation.title: How perspectives change across time
differentiation.activity: Students select a topic represented in texts from at least three historical periods. They investigate the contexts surrounding each text, analyze changes in language and assumptions, and develop an interpretation explaining continuity and change in the perspectives represented.
differentiation.scaffolds: Require students to avoid treating historical periods as uniform or assuming that one author's perspective represents an entire society. Provide feedback on the distinction between historical evidence and generalization.
differentiation.success: Students construct a defensible interpretation supported by multiple texts and contextual sources, explaining both continuity and change without oversimplifying historical perspectives.

questions.prompt: Two articles describe the same proposed transportation project. One emphasizes reduced commuting times, while the other emphasizes the displacement of nearby residents. Which statement best explains the difference between the articles?
options: One article must be factually incorrect.
The articles establish different perspectives by emphasizing different consequences of the project.
The articles necessarily address different topics.
The articles demonstrate that evidence cannot support an argument.
questions.answer: B
questions.rationale: The articles address the same project but frame it through different priorities and consequences. Their perspectives should be evaluated using the evidence each provides.

questions.prompt: Which approach provides the strongest evidence for an interpretation of an author's perspective?
options: Assuming the author's beliefs based on the author's age.
Identifying whether the reader agrees with the author's conclusion.
Analyzing recurring language choices, selected evidence, and the organization of the text.
Determining whether the text is longer than other texts on the topic.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: An interpretation of perspective should be grounded in observable textual evidence rather than assumptions about the author or the reader's personal agreement.

questions.prompt: A headline describes a new policy as a breakthrough, while another describes the same policy as a costly experiment. Which concept best explains this difference?
options: Framing
Chronology
Attribution
Corroboration
questions.answer: A
questions.rationale: The headlines frame the policy differently through evaluative language that encourages readers to interpret the policy in particular ways.

questions.prompt: A video review includes the statement: This video is sponsored by the manufacturer of the product being reviewed. What can a reader or viewer reasonably conclude?
options: Every statement in the video is false.
The creator has disclosed a commercial relationship relevant to interpreting the review.
The manufacturer wrote every word of the review.
The review cannot contain useful information.
questions.answer: B
questions.rationale: The sponsorship establishes a commercial relationship. It does not, by itself, establish that the information is false or that the sponsor controlled every editorial decision.

questions.prompt: Which feature most clearly identifies an overt commercial influence in a digital article?
options: The article contains photographs.
The article was published recently.
The article includes a disclosure stating that the publisher receives commissions from purchases made through its links.
The article contains an author's biography.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: The affiliate disclosure explicitly identifies a financial relationship associated with the article.

questions.prompt: Why should readers investigate the historical circumstances surrounding a text's creation?
options: Historical context guarantees that the author's claims are accurate.
Historical context eliminates the need to analyze the text itself.
Historical context helps explain the conditions, assumptions, and events that may influence the author's perspective and choices.
Historical context proves that all people living during the same period shared identical beliefs.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: Historical context can clarify the circumstances shaping a text without replacing textual analysis or implying that everyone in a period held the same perspective.

questions.prompt: A historian and an epidemiologist investigate the same public health crisis. The historian examines government records and personal accounts, while the epidemiologist analyzes disease transmission data. What best explains the difference?
options: The researchers have different disciplinary contexts that influence their questions and methods.
Only the historian can produce credible information.
Only the epidemiologist can communicate a perspective.
The researchers cannot contribute to a shared understanding of the crisis.
questions.answer: A
questions.rationale: Different disciplines investigate different aspects of a subject through distinct methods and evidence standards. Their findings may contribute complementary insights.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph structure best demonstrates synthesis?
options: A paragraph summarizing Source A, followed by unrelated paragraphs summarizing Sources B and C.
A paragraph presenting only the student's opinion.
A paragraph organizing evidence from several sources around a shared claim and explaining where the sources agree or differ.
A paragraph copying several quotations without explaining their relationships.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: Synthesis organizes information around relationships among ideas and integrates sources to develop a coherent understanding.

questions.prompt: Which action is most appropriate when two credible sources reach different conclusions?
options: Discard the source that disagrees with the student's opinion.
Assume that one source is intentionally misleading.
Compare their evidence, methods, definitions, contexts, and limitations.
Average their conclusions without investigating the differences.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: Differences may result from methods, evidence, definitions, contexts, or the scope of the research. A responsible researcher investigates these factors.

questions.prompt: A student researching the health effects of sleep finds a peer-reviewed study, a mattress advertisement, a personal blog, and a medical association's evidence-based guidance. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: All four sources are equally credible for every research claim.
The advertisement is automatically false because it has a commercial purpose.
The student should evaluate each source's expertise, evidence, purpose, relevance, and limitations before determining how it can contribute to the research.
The student should select the source with the most appealing visual design.
questions.answer: C
questions.rationale: Credibility depends on the source's relationship to the particular question, the quality of its evidence, its methods, and relevant purposes or interests.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between identifying an author's perspective and analyzing how the author establishes that perspective.
questions.answer: Identifying perspective involves describing the position or interpretive lens communicated by the author. Analyzing its development requires explaining how specific language, evidence, organization, examples, or rhetorical choices establish and reinforce that perspective.
questions.rationale: A complete response distinguishes recognition from evidence-based analysis of the text's construction.

questions.prompt: Explain why identifying commercial influence in a digital text does not automatically establish that the text is inaccurate.
questions.answer: A commercial relationship may influence the selection or presentation of information, but the accuracy of particular claims must still be evaluated through evidence and independent verification. Disclosure helps readers understand a relevant interest without proving that every claim is false.
questions.rationale: Students should distinguish potential influence from demonstrated inaccuracy and explain the importance of evaluating evidence.

questions.prompt: Two writers discuss the same historical event, one writing during the event and the other writing fifty years later. Explain two contextual factors that could influence their different perspectives.
questions.answer: The writers may have access to different evidence, experience different social or political circumstances, work within different cultural expectations, or interpret the event with different knowledge of its consequences. A strong response explains how specific contextual differences could influence the resulting texts.
questions.rationale: Students should connect plausible contextual factors to perspective and text creation without assuming that chronological distance automatically guarantees accuracy.

questions.prompt: Explain how a scientific perspective and an ethical perspective might contribute different insights to a discussion of genetic engineering.
questions.answer: A scientific perspective might examine methods, biological mechanisms, effectiveness, and measurable risks. An ethical perspective might examine consent, fairness, responsibility, and acceptable uses. Together, these perspectives can contribute a more comprehensive understanding of the issue.
questions.rationale: Students should identify differences in disciplinary questions and evidence while explaining how the perspectives can complement one another.

questions.prompt: A student has written four paragraphs, each summarizing a different source. Explain how the student could revise the writing to demonstrate synthesis.
questions.answer: The student could organize paragraphs around shared ideas, questions, or claims instead of individual sources. Within each paragraph, the student could integrate relevant evidence from multiple sources, explain agreements and disagreements, and develop a conclusion that reflects their relationships.
questions.rationale: The response should demonstrate understanding that synthesis involves connecting ideas rather than merely placing summaries next to one another.

questions.prompt: Read two teacher-selected texts presenting different perspectives on the same topic. Analyze how each text establishes its perspective and explain how at least two rhetorical choices in each text may influence audience perceptions.
questions.answer: A successful response accurately identifies both perspectives, analyzes specific rhetorical choices from each text, explains their effects on audience interpretation, and compares the texts using relevant evidence.
questions.rationale: Assess accuracy of interpretation, specificity of evidence, depth of rhetorical analysis, and quality of cross-text comparison.

questions.prompt: Examine a teacher-selected sponsored digital or audiovisual text. Identify evidence of overt commercial influence and explain how that relationship may affect the construction or presentation of the text. Distinguish confirmed information from inference.
questions.answer: A strong response identifies a visible disclosure or other documented commercial relationship, analyzes specific presentation choices, explains possible implications for audience interpretation, and avoids unsupported claims about motives or factual accuracy.
questions.rationale: Assess identification of overt commercial influence, evidence-based reasoning, and the ability to distinguish observation from inference.

questions.prompt: Compare two texts addressing a shared issue from different historical periods. Use credible contextual research to explain how historical circumstances influence the perspectives and construction of both texts.
questions.answer: A successful response accurately represents each text, identifies relevant historical circumstances, connects those circumstances to specific textual choices, and explains meaningful similarities or differences across time.
questions.rationale: Assess historical accuracy, textual evidence, contextual reasoning, and avoidance of unsupported generalizations.

questions.prompt: Investigate a focused question using at least four credible sources. Write an explanatory synthesis that integrates information from the sources, identifies meaningful agreements or disagreements, and develops a conclusion supported by the available evidence.
questions.answer: A strong response presents a focused question, organizes information around meaningful ideas, accurately integrates multiple credible sources, explains their relationships, attributes evidence appropriately, and acknowledges relevant limitations or uncertainty.
questions.rationale: Evaluate source credibility, accuracy, integration, organization, reasoning, attribution, and the quality of the evidence-based conclusion.

questions.prompt: Create a research briefing on a complex contemporary or historical issue. Include at least three relevant perspectives, explain the historical or disciplinary contexts shaping them, identify any documented commercial influences in selected sources, and synthesize credible evidence into a defensible conclusion.
questions.answer: Successful work demonstrates accurate comparison of perspectives, contextual analysis, responsible identification of commercial influence where present, credible research, coherent synthesis, appropriate attribution, and a conclusion proportionate to the available evidence.
questions.rationale: Use separate rubric criteria for perspective analysis, contextual understanding, media literacy, source evaluation, synthesis, and communication.

evidence: An evidence-based explanation of an author's or speaker's perspective.
Annotations identifying how diction, tone, framing, organization, and evidence develop perspective.
A comparison of multiple texts addressing a shared topic.
An analysis explaining how rhetorical choices influence audience perceptions or beliefs.
Accurate identification of overt commercial influences in digital or audiovisual examples.
A media analysis distinguishing documented commercial relationships from unsupported assumptions.
A contextual explanation connecting historical circumstances to specific features of a text.
A comparison explaining how perspectives change or remain consistent across historical periods.
A disciplinary comparison identifying differences in questions, methods, evidence, and interpretations.
A focused research question supported by relevant and credible source selection.
Source evaluation notes documenting expertise, evidence, relevance, transparency, and limitations.
A synthesis matrix identifying relationships among ideas from multiple sources.
A research paragraph integrating evidence from more than one source.
An extended synthesis organized around ideas rather than individual source summaries.
Accurate representation of source agreement, disagreement, qualification, and uncertainty.
Appropriate attribution of information, quotations, paraphrases, and interpretations.
A defensible conclusion supported by multiple credible sources.
Independent application of perspective analysis and source evaluation to unfamiliar texts.
instruction: Begin with paired texts addressing familiar topics so students can recognize how different perspectives shape communication.
Explicitly distinguish topic, perspective, purpose, tone, narrative point of view, and bias.
Model how to infer perspective from observable textual evidence rather than assumptions about an author's identity or motives.
Teach students to examine diction, examples, evidence, organization, framing, and patterns of emphasis.
Use comparison organizers that require students to analyze how perspectives are developed, not merely identify whether authors agree.
Include texts representing different genres, modes, cultural experiences, historical periods, and disciplinary contexts.
Teach students to recognize that a text can communicate a perspective without making an explicitly argumentative claim.
Analyze headlines, images, captions, video editing, music, and other multimodal features when examining digital and audiovisual texts.
Introduce commercial influence through authentic, age-appropriate examples of sponsorships, affiliate disclosures, advertisements, and product placement.
Use current authoritative consumer guidance to clarify common commercial disclosures.
Distinguish overt commercial influence from speculative claims about hidden financial relationships.
Teach students to evaluate the accuracy of sponsored content independently of its commercial status.
Provide relevant historical context before asking students to interpret historically distant texts.
Model how to connect a documented contextual circumstance to a specific textual feature.
Compare texts across historical periods to examine continuity, change, and competing interpretations.
Avoid presenting any single author as representative of an entire historical period, culture, or community.
Introduce disciplinary context by comparing the questions and methods used by different fields of study.
Collaborate with teachers in science, social studies, and other content areas to develop interdisciplinary text sets.
Teach students to formulate focused, researchable questions before collecting sources.
Model source evaluation through expertise, evidence, transparency, relevance, and independent corroboration.
Use school library databases and credible institutional resources to support research.
Teach lateral reading as a strategy for investigating unfamiliar authors, organizations, and claims.
Use synthesis matrices organized by themes, questions, claims, or findings rather than only by source.
Model how to integrate multiple sources within a single analytical paragraph.
Teach transitions that communicate agreement, contrast, qualification, extension, and uncertainty.
Require students to accurately attribute source information and distinguish their own conclusions from source claims.
Provide opportunities for students to revise source-by-source summaries into coherent syntheses.
Assess the quality of reasoning and source integration rather than rewarding the number of sources alone.
Use authentic research questions connected to students' academic interests, communities, and future decisions.
Gradually remove scaffolds so students independently analyze perspective, investigate context, evaluate media, and synthesize research.
watchFor: Confusing the topic of a text with the perspective communicated about that topic.
Identifying an author's perspective without supporting the interpretation with textual evidence.
Assuming that perspective and bias are interchangeable terms.
Treating every perspective as equally supported regardless of the available evidence.
Equating disagreement with dishonesty or inaccuracy.
Assuming an author's perspective solely from personal identity, nationality, occupation, or historical period.
Confusing an author's perspective with the perspective of a fictional narrator or character.
Treating an author's stated purpose as the only evidence of perspective.
Identifying rhetorical choices without explaining how they influence audience interpretation.
Comparing texts only by listing similarities and differences without analyzing their significance.
Assuming that omitted information was intentionally concealed without supporting evidence.
Treating commercial influence as proof that a text contains false information.
Failing to recognize explicit sponsorship or affiliate disclosures.
Assuming that every visible brand or product appearance establishes a paid commercial arrangement.
Making unsupported accusations about hidden sponsorships or financial motives.
Confusing popularity, professional design, or high engagement with credibility.
Using historical background as a substitute for close reading.
Assuming that all people in a historical period shared the same perspective.
Applying contemporary assumptions to historical texts without considering relevant circumstances.
Assuming that later interpretations are automatically more accurate than earlier accounts.
Treating disciplinary differences as evidence that one discipline is inherently more credible than another.
Selecting sources only because they agree with an initial opinion.
Relying on a source's reputation without evaluating its relevance to the specific claim.
Using outdated information when the research question requires current evidence.
Treating source evaluation as a mechanical checklist without considering context.
Confusing a collection of source summaries with synthesis.
Organizing an entire research response around individual sources rather than meaningful ideas.
Forcing sources into agreement when their evidence or conclusions differ.
Presenting disagreement as a simple two-sided debate when the issue involves multiple perspectives.
Combining evidence without explaining the relationships among sources.
Quoting extensively without analysis or interpretation.
Failing to attribute paraphrased information.
Drawing conclusions that exceed the scope or strength of the available evidence.
Ignoring uncertainty, limitations, or unresolved questions.
Assessing research primarily through formatting or source quantity rather than the quality of evidence and reasoning.

10.T.C.2.a.focus: Compare and contrast varying perspectives across texts
10.T.C.2.a.studentFriendly: I can compare how different authors and speakers present the same topic and explain how their language, evidence, and organization influence what audiences think or believe.
know: Perspective is the position or interpretive lens through which a subject is presented.
Authors establish perspective through language, selected details, evidence, examples, organization, and rhetorical choices.
Perspective may be explicit or implicit.
Framing emphasizes particular aspects of a subject and influences interpretation.
Authors may communicate different perspectives while addressing the same topic.
Perspective differs from narrative point of view, tone, purpose, and bias.
An interpretation of perspective requires textual evidence.
Rhetorical choices can influence perceptions, beliefs, emotions, and judgments.
understand: Different perspectives can reveal contrasting assumptions, priorities, experiences, and interpretations.
The construction of a text influences how its audience understands the subject.
Authors may shape perceptions through selective emphasis, organization, and framing.
A meaningful comparison explains how perspectives are established and why differences matter.
Perspective analysis should distinguish evidence from unsupported speculation about motives.
Readers can evaluate the quality of evidence without assuming that disagreement establishes inaccuracy.
do: Identify the perspective communicated in a text.
Support an interpretation of perspective with specific textual evidence.

Use revision tasks that allow students to experiment with different perspectives while maintaining factual accuracy.

10.T.C.2.b.focus: Identify overtly commercial influences in audiovisual and digital texts
10.T.C.2.b.studentFriendly: I can recognize when advertisements, sponsorships, affiliate relationships, or other visible commercial influences are connected to digital or audiovisual content, and explain why those relationships matter when I interpret the message.
know: Commercial influence involves financial or business interests connected to a text's creation, presentation, or distribution.
Advertisements, sponsorships, paid endorsements, affiliate marketing, and product placement are forms of commercial communication.
Commercial relationships may be identified through explicit disclosures, sponsorship labels, affiliate notices, or other documented evidence.
Digital content can combine entertainment, information, persuasion, and commercial purposes.
Native advertising may resemble surrounding editorial or informational content.
A disclosed commercial relationship is not the same as evidence that a claim is false.
Visible brand appearances do not always establish paid product placement.
Source accuracy should be evaluated through evidence and independent verification.
understand: Commercial relationships may influence the topics, products, evidence, language, and presentation choices used in a text.
Recognizing overt commercial influence helps audiences interpret the purposes and interests connected to a message.
Commercial content can contain accurate and useful information.
A responsible evaluation distinguishes confirmed financial relationships from unsupported speculation.
Media literacy requires examining how content is constructed as well as what it claims.
Disclosures help audiences recognize relevant commercial relationships.
do: Identify overt advertisements and sponsorship labels in digital or audiovisual content.
Recognize affiliate disclosures, paid partnership notices, and other explicit commercial signals.
Distinguish informational content from overt advertising when sufficient evidence is available.
Identify documented commercial relationships connected to a text.
Explain how commercial influence may shape presentation, emphasis, or audience expectations.
Compare sponsored content with independently produced content addressing a similar topic.
Evaluate claims using evidence rather than commercial status alone.
Distinguish direct observation from inference about commercial influence.
Use credible consumer guidance to interpret common disclosure practices.
targets: I can recognize overt commercial influences in digital and audiovisual texts.
I can identify sponsorships, advertisements, and affiliate disclosures.

evidence: Correct identification of visible advertisements and sponsorship disclosures.
Accurate explanation of an affiliate or paid partnership relationship.
An analysis of how documented commercial influence may affect presentation.

A media evaluation distinguishing commercial evidence from speculation.
Independent verification of a claim made within commercial content.
watchFor: Assuming that sponsored content is automatically inaccurate.
Failing to recognize explicit commercial disclosures.

10.T.C.2.c.focus: Explain how historical and disciplinary contexts influence perspectives and text creation
10.T.C.2.c.studentFriendly: I can explain how the time period, circumstances, and field of study surrounding a text influence the author's perspective and the way the text is created.
know: Historical context includes events, institutions, beliefs, technologies, social conditions, and cultural circumstances surrounding a text's creation.
Disciplinary context includes the questions, methods, evidence standards, vocabulary, and purposes of a field of study.
Authors and speakers may respond to events, controversies, institutions, and expectations of their time.
Perspectives may change as knowledge, social conditions, technologies, and institutions change.
Different disciplines may investigate the same topic through different methods and kinds of evidence.
Texts can reflect, challenge, or complicate the assumptions of their historical or disciplinary contexts.
A historical period or discipline contains multiple perspectives rather than a single uniform viewpoint.
Contextual interpretation requires credible evidence about the circumstances being discussed.
understand: Texts are shaped by the circumstances in which they are created.
Historical context can clarify the significance of an author's choices without replacing textual analysis.
Disciplinary context influences what questions authors ask, what evidence they value, and how they communicate findings.
Comparing texts across time can reveal continuity, change, and competing interpretations.
Different disciplinary perspectives may contribute complementary insights to a complex issue.
An author's perspective may challenge rather than simply reflect dominant historical or disciplinary assumptions.
Responsible contextual analysis avoids unsupported generalizations about entire societies, cultures, or periods.
do: Identify relevant historical circumstances surrounding a text's creation.

Connect specific contextual factors to language, evidence, organization, or rhetorical choices.
Compare perspectives represented in texts from different historical periods.
Explain how historical changes influence perspectives and text creation.

Collaborate with content-area teachers to develop authentic disciplinary comparisons.
Require students to explain contextual relationships rather than merely list historical facts.

evidence: Accurate identification of relevant historical circumstances.

10.T.C.2.d.focus: Synthesize information from credible sources to answer research questions
10.T.C.2.d.studentFriendly: I can investigate a question that interests me, find several credible sources, connect their information and perspectives, and develop a well-supported answer that explains what I learned.
know: A focused research question establishes the purpose and scope of an investigation.
Credible sources demonstrate relevant expertise, evidence, transparency, appropriate methods, and accountability.
Source credibility depends on the relationship between the source and the particular research question.
A variety of sources can provide complementary information, evidence, and perspectives.
Synthesis integrates ideas from multiple sources into a coherent understanding or argument.
Summary communicates the central ideas of a source, while synthesis explains relationships among sources.
Sources may agree, disagree, qualify, extend, or complicate one another.
A synthesis matrix organizes information according to shared questions, themes, claims, or findings.
Quotation, paraphrase, and summary are methods of integrating source information.
Attribution identifies the origins of information and ideas.
Research conclusions should reflect the scope, quality, and limitations of the available evidence.
Responsible researchers acknowledge uncertainty and unresolved questions.
understand: Effective research begins with a meaningful question rather than a predetermined conclusion.
Using multiple credible sources can deepen understanding and reveal limitations that a single source might not address.
Credibility is determined through evidence and relevance rather than agreement with personal beliefs.
Different sources may contribute different kinds of information to the same research question.
Synthesis requires explaining relationships among ideas rather than merely collecting information.
Meaningful disagreement among credible sources can become an important part of a research conclusion.
Accurate attribution supports intellectual honesty and allows readers to evaluate evidence.
A defensible conclusion may acknowledge that the available evidence does not completely resolve a question.

evidence: A focused and researchable question.
A collection of relevant and credible sources.
